This, then, is the move from contingency to necessity which “constitutes the destiny as well as the drama of love.” It is my (im)modest claim—developed elsewhere—that “drama” is a significant word here, and that the comedy of love, or love as comedy, entails a different logic. But if it is indeed to

[SOURCE PAGE 135]

work, the comedy of love is a much more demanding genre than the tragedy or drama of love. (And perhaps the same could be said for political events, namely, that a certain revolutionary “taste for drama” could well be something of a problem.) Lacan’s pessimistic conclusion in the quote above is of course not unrelated to the concept that Badiou introduces at this precise point—at the point of the question “What happens after the Event?”—namely, the concept of fidelity (not simply to our lover, but to the Event of our love encounter). Fidelity, and not just the Event itself, is what can eventually make a difference. Lacan’s reserve at this point could be attributed to his general “pessimism,” or even to something rooted in his political views. But the actual emancipatory implications of the Lacanian theory are in no way confined by these political stances. This is why I am tempted to put forward the following suggestion.

What if we reintroduced here the notion of a “new signifier” as precisely that which could make it possible, in this case, to build something on the basis of a love encounter, without obscuring the contingency of (its) being?

A love (encounter) is not simply about everything falling into its rightful place. A love encounter is not simply about a contingent match between two different pathologies, about two individuals being lucky enough to encounter in each other what “works for them.” Rather, love is what makes it work. Love does something to us. It makes, or allows for, the cause of our desire to condescend to, to coincide with, our lover. And the affect of this is surprise—only this surprise, and not simply our infatuation, is the sign of love proper. It is the sign of the subject, of the subjective figure of love. It says not simply: “You are it!,” but rather: “How surprising that you are it!” Or, in a simpler formula of how love operates: How surprising that you are you!

In order to develop this in a more concrete way, it could be helpful to make a short digression and look at what Clément Rosset says about love in his book Le Régime des passions. Playing on the double meaning of the French word régime—system (of government) and diet)—Rosset develops his criticism of the notion of passion, which he sees as a morbid craving for an unreal (derealized, nonexistent or unattainable) object. Hence a passionate love, in contrast to “real love,” always aims at objects that it cannot really have (and goes to great lengths to ensure just that); it is a passionate relationship with an unreal object. (Even if there is a concrete person behind it, as in Racine’s Phaedra, this person is precisely irrelevant as a real person.) This is a love for an object the approach to which and enjoyment of which are infinitely deferred. According to Rosset, this amorous passion (which could be more appropriately called the passion of desire) is the opposite of love; it is like a war machine dedicated to paralyzing and forbidding. Hence

[SOURCE PAGE 136]

Phaedra “elects an object the enjoyment of which she forbids herself (I would even say that she elects him so as not to enjoy him), and then draws masochistic enjoyment from her very pain” (Rosset 2001, 16). For this is the other side of the “passion diet”: it involves enjoyment not in the object of passion, but in the passionate dieting itself. (This is why Rosset rejects Saint-Simon’s famous formula “Nothing great happens without passion,” and replaces it with “Nothing mediocre happens without passion.”) Rosset detects a similar passion structure (that is, an unappeasable craving for, and fascination with, an obscure and unreal object) in avarice and in the passion of collectors: the real objects of these passions don’t really count. The miser never enjoys his treasure (or its value): “The miser is fascinated by the aura of unreality in which he makes his money swim, but not by the money itself” (ibid., 17). What thus defines passion, according to Rosset, is less a search for something than a quest for an object defined by two fundamental conditions: that it is obscure and indefinable, and at the same time outside any useful reach (that is, both out of reach and useless). And the more this is so, the greater the passion in its morbid self-perpetuating logic. This is precisely what makes Rosset link the logic of passion to what is the central topic of his philosophical work, namely, the theme of “the real and its double.” To put it briefly: passion marks the hold that the fantasy of the double has over the perception of the real, the fascination with the absence provoked by the undesirable presence of a real which does not satisfy (or no longer satisfies) us, that is to say, the choice of the unreal to the detriment of the real. And one could add here that “revolutionary passion” actually often functions precisely in this way: as a passion for the “revolution” itself, rather than for patiently building a different world.

There is, however, something that Rosset skims over too quickly in his theory of passion, as well as in his theory of the double as simply an illusory redoubling of the real. In the opposition between the real object and the perverse enjoyment (in its deferral), real love is not simply on the side of the “real object” (as fully coinciding with itself). Moreover, one should insist that there is a certain degree of derealization or detachment involved in any real love, and this constitutes the very basis of the encounter and of the relationship with a concrete, “real” person. Paradoxically, this is something that Rosset himself very perspicaciously observes, without accepting the immediate consequences of this observation for his theory:

Real love demands the reality of the loved person. Besides, the coincidence thanks to which a loved object is at the same time an existing object is, rather curiously, an inexhaustible subject of wonder for the lovers…: it is no longer “you are here” that counts, but the fact that “you are you.” (Rosset 2001, 28)

[SOURCE PAGE 137]

This is precisely the formula we arrived at in our discussion above. Real love necessarily wonders at the coincidence of the loved (desired) object with an existing object. And this wondering is the affect of love proper.

In the terms of Rosset’s arguments, this implies that there is something of the order of surprising coincidence that takes place also in real love, and hence presupposes a minimal difference or split—this split does not occur only with the illusory distortion (reduplication of the real, as he argues). And, as a matter of fact, the wonder here is no less comical than the one evoked in one of the jokes Freud quotes in his book on Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious: “He wondered how it is that cats have two holes cut in their skin precisely at the place where their eyes are” (Freud 1976, 97).

In order for the real lover to be nothing but the coincidence with herself, as Rosset himself maintains, there also needs to be a split, involving a minimal difference. It is precisely this minimal difference on account of which it makes sense to say, not Je est un autre (Rimbaud), but tu est toi, “you are you(rself),” which is the very condition (and form) of real love. It is not only that real love demands the reality of the loved person, it is also, and primarily, precisely about this coincidence of the same as the other side of its non-coincidence, made visible by the amorous encounter in the strong sense of the word. The split and the coincidence appear at the same time. Or: split appears as coincidence; they are, strictly speaking, one and the same.

In other words, we can agree with Rosset that “real love” is not the love that I would call sublime, the love in which we let ourselves be completely dazzled or “blinded” by an abstract dimension of the loved object, so that we no longer see, or can’t bear to see, its concrete existence (and its always somewhat ridiculous, banal aspect). This kind of “sublime love” indeed necessitates and generates a radical inaccessibility of the other (which usually takes the form of eternal preliminaries, of an inaccessible object of choice, or the form of an intermittent relationship that enables us to reintroduce the distance appropriate to the inaccessible, and thereby to “resublimate” the object after each “use”). But neither is real love simply something that takes its object “such as it is,” in the sense of homogeneity and (uninterrupted) continuity of its presence as real. It is only at the moment when we fall in love that a loved object “coincides” with an existing object, and this coincidence marks a break in the continuity of our (and our lover’s) reality. This paradoxical—or, indeed, comical—coincidence is precisely what tears us (and our lover) from the continuity of our presence in reality, and it does so by (re)installing us there, as if for the first time.

An exchange in Marx Brothers’ A Night at the Opera spells this out most directly. After sitting with another woman for quite a while, Groucho (Driftwood) comes to Mrs. Claypool’s table (she has been waiting for him all this time), and the following dialogue ensues:

[SOURCE PAGE 138]

Driftwood (Groucho):  That woman? Do you know why I sat with her? Mrs. Claypool (Margaret Dumont):  No— Driftwood:  Because she reminded me of you. Mrs. Claypool:  Really? Driftwood:  Of course! That’s why I’m sitting here with you. Because you remind me of you. Your eyes, your throat, your lips, everything about you reminds me of you, except you. How do you account for that?

Comic subjects are best situated to produce genuine formulas of love. Indeed, come to think of it, is there any better answer to the impossible question: “Why do you love me?” than: “Because you remind me of yourself”? Now, how do we relate all this to our discussion above? One way of understanding the notion of the “new signifier” would be precisely to see it as a signifier capable of naming, and hence sustaining, the minimal difference (contingency) on account of which my lover keeps reminding me of himself. In other words, to see it as precisely that which prevents the shift of negation that Lacan points out, the shift from “stops not being written” to “doesn’t stop being written.” What happens in this shift is that the impossibility disappears, and is simply replaced by necessity; but this disappearance of impossibility is not its solution, but its repression or foreclosure; hence the closing up of the very gap that made its “evental” solution possible in the first place. In love, the impossible happens, and it is from there on that we must continue and work with what has happened, instead of assuming that from now on the impossible is (or should be) simply replaced by the possible and, indeed, necessary. Since we have already ventured quite a long way onto the terrain of concrete examples, we can take a step further here and suggest a concrete example of a “new signifier” in the case of an amorous circumstance—with the obvious risk of the example striking us as rather banal with respect to our sublime expectations of what this new signifier might be. We shall take the risk. So what would be an example of a signifier capable of naming, and hence sustaining, the minimal difference (contingency) on account of which my lover keeps reminding me of himself? An example of a signifier that would prevent the gap of the “impossible” from simply disappearing from the scene (and returning in the Real)? Could we not say that a possible example of this would be the way in which a nickname sometimes functions in love relationships? And by this I certainly do not mean a “cute name” that one can pick from a list of such names, I mean a name that really names something in the relationship; a name that provides the signifier of the very (dis) junction of love object and existing object in a concrete love relationship. A name that works, works at generating and maintaining the space for construction at the precarious point of the Event. Such (nick)names (obviously, not all love nicknames work in this way, and there can also be something other than

[SOURCE PAGE 139]

a nickname that does the job) usually have a comic sparkle to them, and this sparkle goes some distance in distracting the pathos of love as destiny.

Names, words—don’t we have enough of those?

We started with sex (in its “impossibility”), and ended up with love in its evental dimension—which does not take us very far if it does not find its ally in some sort of signifying invention. This is where I want to stop. There are of course more general conclusions that one could develop from here, but I will restrict myself to just one brief remark. We often attribute the source of the evils of our time to the accelerating flow of (“just”) words, speculation; to the lack of involvement with real things, real life, real experiences, and real emotions. Yet the problem is perhaps different: we have not lost the Real (which we never “had”), we are losing the capacity of naming that can have real effects, because it “hits” the right spot, the (dis)junction between the necessary and the Real (impossible). In all the profusion of words and more words, we lack the words that work. (Not what linguistics calls performatives, but words that can affect the economy of being because they come from the workings of this economy.) The turn to the Real (for example, to “real experience”) is part of the ideological warfare that diverts us from the only way in which we can touch something of the Real, which is precisely with the right word (and not simply with more words). The right word is not the same thing as a correct word, and it is certainly not about someone “being right” (or not); it is not simply the word that conveys, for example, the factual truth of what is going on. This is not about “efficiency” either. It is about words that name something about our reality for the first time, and hence make this something an object of the world, and of thought. There can be words and descriptions of reality prior to it, and there always are. But then there comes a word that gives us access to reality in a whole different way. It is not a correct description of a reality; it introduces a new reality. When Marx wrote that “the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles,” this is was not a description of social history that was more accurate than other descriptions. The concept of the class struggle is an example of a “new signifier,” one that reveals a hitherto invisible dimension of social reality, and gives us tools to think it. It does so because it names the point where the impossibility of social justice gets disentangled from the necessity to repeat this impossibility.

[SOURCE PAGE 140]


# Conclusion — From Adam's Navel to Dream's Navel

[SOURCE PAGE 141]

After this excursion into the possible philosophical (and political) implications of the psychoanalytic concept of sexuality, let us conclude with what seems to be its most daring implication. Namely, that sexuality (as linked to the unconscious) is the point of a short circuit between ontology and epistemology: it is because of what is missing (“fallen out”) from the signifying structuring of being that the unconscious, as a form of knowledge, relates to the impossibility of being involved in, and “transmitted” by, sexuality.

The theory that there exists a singular short circuit between ontological and epistemological dimensions is, of course, a very strong “philosophical” claim. Yet Freud himself suggested something of the sort in his account of the link between sexuality and knowledge: if sexuality is the drive of knowledge, it is not simply because we are curious about sex, or because we sublimate the lack of sex with a passion for knowledge. For the lack at stake is not a possible lack of sex, but a lack at the very heart of sex, or, more precisely, it concerns sex as the very structural incompleteness of being.

One of Freud’s major theories concerns sexuality as the realm within which the quest (desire) for knowledge takes off. This Freudian genealogy of the passion for knowledge is in itself complex and intriguing, but its basic outline would be as follows:1 There is no original drive for knowledge. It surfaces at points of existential difficulty: for example, when children feel threatened by the fact (or the possibility) of acquiring a sibling. Sexuality very soon becomes an obvious player in all questions about being (there) of oneself and of others. It enters the stage with the question of being (“How do we come to be?”), and it enters as negativity, as the unsatisfactory character of all possible positive answers. For while it is obviously involved in the becoming of being, sexuality nevertheless provides no point of attachment, no anchoring point, in the explication of being (as being). Moreover, for the inquisitive

[SOURCE PAGE 142]

infant, sexuality is often bound up with stories and myths, embarrassment and avoidance, sometimes even with disgust and punishment. Before we sigh that, well, this is again all about our petty little family stories and structures, it is crucial to acknowledge that the true question only begins at this point. It is not that these “family structures” can explain the Real of sexuality, but rather that something in the latter can explain, or point to, the gap that drives these structures. The embarrassment at and covering up of sexuality (by adults) should not be taken as self-explanatory, that is, as explained by the “traditional” cultural ban on sexuality, but rather the other way around. As I keep insisting, the cause of embarrassment in sexuality is not simply something which is there, on display in it, but on the contrary something that is not there, and is (or would be) of the order of knowledge. The fairytales with which we explain sexuality to children are there not so much in order to mask and distort the realistic explanation, but to mask the fact that there is no realistic explanation, and that even the most exhaustive scientific explanation lacks the signifier that would account for the sexual as sexual. What is at stake with this lack is thus not a missing piece of knowledge about the sexual (as a full entity in itself); what is at stake is that (drive) sexuality and knowledge are structured around a fundamental negativity, which unites them at the point of the unconscious. The unconscious is the concept of an inherent link between sexuality and knowledge in their very negativity.

The conclusion we can draw from all this would thus be the following: Whenever it comes to social, cultural, or religious covering up of sexuality, we can be sure that it never covers up simply what is there (for example, the sexual organs), but also (and perhaps primarily) something which is not there; it also covers up some fundamental ambiguity which is, from the outset, of a metaphysical order. In other words: the more we try to think the sexual as sexual (that is, the more we try to think it only for “what it is,” without censorship and embellishments), the quicker we find ourselves in the element of pure and profound metaphysics. This is why there is no “neutral” way to speak about sex—even if we pretend not to hide anything, and speak only of facts, something else seems to get added, or to disappear.… A vivid and direct illustration of this can be found in the form of a problem that early artists faced when they painted Adam and Eve, a problem that relates these questions to our earlier discussion of realism. The problem the artists faced was the following: Should they portray the first couple with or without navels? Adam was molded from spit and clay, Eve from Adam’s rib. They were not born of women, so how could they have navels? Yet they looked strange without them: they were the first humans, and they should look like (other) humans. But if as humans they were created in God’s image, God also has to have a navel, which generates new conceptual difficulties.…(This

[SOURCE PAGE 143]

illustrates the dilemma that Gosse was facing when he was trying to reconcile the geological age of fossils with God’s creation according to Genesis: his answer was that when God created Adam, he also created the navel, that is to say, his “ancestry.”…) So the problem the artists faced was quite real; and they often dodged the question by extending fig leaves so that they covered not only the sexual organs, but the lower belly as well.

Is not this extending of the fig leaves to hide more than just sexual organs a perfect illustration of the argument I am making here? Namely, that by covering up “the sexual,” one always also—and perhaps primarily?—covers up something else, something that is not there and which tends to raise some deeply metaphysical issues and ambiguities. And it should come as no surprise that it is precisely this additional point that is the principal locus of myths and fantasies about procreation and about (our) origins. Different theological theories surrounding the issue of Adam’s navel—for example, the “Pre-Umbilist,” “Mid-Umbilist,” and “Post-Umbilist” theories—constitute fascinating reading.

The extended fig leaf covers not simply the sexual, but the navel as the elected figure of the scar left by the lapse of being—the lapse of being involved in sexuation (and sexual reproduction). If sexuality seems to exist only on the ontic level, and to have no proper ontological dignity, the reason is not that it corresponds to nothing on the ontological level, but rather that it corresponds to a gap inside this ontological level.

And, speaking of navels, it is of course no coincidence that we find in Freud (in The Interpretation of Dreams) the famous, as well as curious, expression: der Nabel des Traums, “the dream’s navel,” related not to what we can know, but to the hole in the very net of knowledge that can be laid out in the analytic interpretation.

There is often a passage in even the most thoroughly interpreted dream which has to be left obscure; this is because we become aware during the work of interpretation that at that point there is a tangle of dream-thoughts which cannot be unraveled and which moreover adds nothing to our knowledge of the content of the dream. This is the dream’s navel, the spot where it reaches down into the unknown. (Freud 1988, 671)

I would suggest that we should read the term “unknown” not as referring to something “unknown to us,” but in a stronger sense of the gap in knowledge coinciding with the gap in being. We do not know, because there is nothing to know. Yet this “nothing” is inherent to being, and constitutes its irreducible crack; it registers as a peculiar (“negative”) epistemological score, it registers as a peculiar form of knowledge: the unconscious.

In general theoretical terms, we should say of this configuration: it is not that there is one fundamental non-relation and a multiplicity of different relations, determined by the former in a negative way. It is, rather, that every relationship also posits the concrete point of the impossible that determines it. It determines what will be determining it. In this sense we could say that all social relations are concretizations of the non-relation as universal determination of the discursive, which does not exist anywhere outside these concrete (non-)relations. This also means that the non-relation is not the ultimate (ontological) foundation of the discursive, but its surface—it exists and manifests itself only through it. To put it differently: it is not that there is (and remains) a fundamental non-relation which will never be (re)solved by any concrete relation. Rather: every concrete relation de facto resolves the non-relation, but it can resolve it only by positing (“inventing”), together with itself, its own negativity, its own negative condition/impossibility. The non-relation is not something that “insists” and “remains,” but something that is repeated—something that “does not stop not being written” (to use Lacan’s expression). It is not something that resists all writing, and that no writing can actually write—it is inherent to writing, and repeats itself with it.

In the context of the Freudian theory of the sexual seduction of children (and the possible “trauma” related to it), Jean Laplanche has convincingly argued that this kind of alternative is wrong, or too simple. Freud first posited the sexual seduction of children by adults as real, that is to say, as a factual/empirical event in the child’s history, which is then repressed and can become the ground or cause of different symptoms and neurotic disturbances. Later, he abandoned this theory in favor of the theory of the fantasy of seduction: generally speaking, seduction is not an event that takes place in empirical reality, but a fantasy constructed later, in the period of our sexual awareness, and it exists only in the psychic reality of the subject. Approached with the tool of the distinction between material reality and psychic reality (fantasy), the question of sexual seduction leads either to the claim that everything is material seduction (for how exactly are we to isolate and define the latter: does touching a baby’s lips, for example, or its bottom, qualify as seduction?) or to the conclusion that seduction is entirely fantasmatic, mediated by the psychic reality of the one who “feels seduced.” Laplanche’s answer to this conflict between raw materialism and psychological idealism is profoundly materialistic in the sense that he recognizes a properly material cause, yet a cause that cannot be reduced to (or deduced from) what has empirically happened in the interaction between the child and the adult. In other words, according to Laplanche, the true trigger of the subsequent constitution of the unconscious lies neither in raw material reality nor in the ideal reality of fantasy, but is the very materiality of a third reality, which is transversal to the other two and

# Alfredo Eidelsztein - The Graph of Desire

## Source and edition note

This file reconstructs Alfredo Eidelsztein's *The Graph of Desire: Using the Work of Jacques Lacan*, first published in English by Karnac Books in 2009. The book is based on recordings of a 1993 postgraduate course, *The Graph of Desire and the Psychoanalytic Clinic*, taught within the Updating Program on Lacanian Psychoanalysis at the Faculty of Psychology, University of Buenos Aires. The English translation is by Florencia F. C. Shanahan, reviewed by Philip Malone.

Eidelsztein treats Lacan's graph of desire as a technical instrument linking psychoanalytic practice to topology, mathematical graph theory, the theory of the signifier, fantasy, drive, jouissance and castration. His sustained textual reference is Lacan's "The Subversion of the Subject and the Dialectic of Desire in the Freudian Unconscious", supplemented by seminars and other writings as he reads them.

This is a secondary Lacanian interpretation, not a transcription of Lacan. Formulations are therefore attributed to Eidelsztein whenever they express his reconstruction, criticism or extension of Lacan. Where Eidelsztein quotes or paraphrases Lacan, the distinction is preserved.

## Coverage of this file

The reconstruction follows the complete conceptual sequence of the Introduction and Chapters 1-15. It preserves the progressive construction of the graph, Eidelsztein's use of topology and graph theory, the major clinical and structural claims, questions and answers, and the important diagrams, mathemes and formulas needed to understand his reading. References are retained at a research-useful level; the printed index is not mechanically reproduced.

## Introduction

Eidelsztein explains that the book is a lightly edited record of a 1993 postgraduate course devoted to the graph of desire and its relation to psychoanalytic practice. The lectures retain their colloquial form rather than being rewritten into a conventional monograph. Throughout the course he repeatedly returns to Lacan's "The Subversion of the Subject and the Dialectic of Desire in the Freudian Unconscious", paraphrasing and quoting it as the central textual anchor.

A methodological issue is already explicit in the Introduction. Eidelsztein considered the available Spanish translation of Lacan problematic in places and sometimes translated passages himself from the French in order to establish what he believed Lacan was asserting. The resulting book is therefore not merely an exposition of an accepted doctrine. It is an exercise in close reading that often turns on terminology, notation, translation and the structural consequences of how a passage is read.

The declared aim is to reopen and deepen the study of Lacan rather than to provide an introductory summary. The form of the book reflects the pedagogical setting: concepts are introduced, tested through questions, reformulated and connected to clinical practice over successive classes.

### Sources used

- Alfredo Eidelsztein, *The Graph of Desire: Using the Work of Jacques Lacan*, Introduction, printed p. vii, project PDF p. 6.

## Chapter 1 - Graph of desire and topology

### The graph as the systematic entrance of topology

Eidelsztein begins by placing the graph of desire within the larger sequence of Lacanian representational devices: models, schemata, graphs, topological surfaces and knots. His claim is that Lacan gives these devices an unusually central place because psychoanalysis requires a way to represent the structure of the speaking subject without simply reproducing ordinary images of a person or mind. Within that series, the graph marks the first systematic use of topology in Lacan's teaching.

He connects this to the history of mathematics. Euler's work on the Königsberg bridges is both a founding moment of graph theory and an important precursor of topology. The point is not historical decoration. Eidelsztein wants the same formal shift, from ordinary spatial intuition to structural relations, to organize the psychoanalytic reading of the subject.

The clinical rationale is stated in terms of the Real, Symbolic and Imaginary. If Lacanian psychoanalysis claims that the subject is structured through these registers, then its theoretical devices and its direction of treatment should themselves respect that structure. A representation dominated by ordinary visual resemblance risks contradicting what it is meant to demonstrate.

Eidelsztein uses Lacan's optical model as his first example. In the model, the Imaginary is associated with the image that captures and deceives the subject; the Real with the inaccessible body; and the Symbolic with virtual space. He rotates the usual arrangement to emphasize Lacan's proposition that the Symbolic determines both the Imaginary and the Real, which stand in an equivalent relation to it.

[FIGURE: Schemas 1 and 2, topography of Real, Symbolic and Imaginary]
Source location: printed p. 3 / PDF p. 9
Type: schematic topography
Description: Schema 1 places I over R on the left side of an oval and S on the right. Schema 2 rotates the relation so S occupies the upper half, while I and R occupy the lower left and lower right.
Labels visible in source: I, R, S.
Directional structure: no arrows; spatial relation is the point.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: the rotation makes visible his claim that Imaginary and Real have an equivalent topological relation to the Symbolic, rather than the Symbolic being merely another component of a three-part picture.
Fidelity note: visually checked against source PDF p. 9.

The optical model also reveals a problem. It uses mirrors to represent both the mirror-stage relation and the big Other. Eidelsztein treats this as an imaginary device in the precise sense of analogy. A mirror resembles or stands in for another mirror relation. Yet the signifier is defined through difference, not resemblance. If one uses an analogical, image-based instrument to establish the determining role of the Symbolic, the form of the explanation undermines the content. He describes this as a kind of denial: the Symbolic is proclaimed determinant while the device of demonstration remains imaginary.

This has a clinical correlate in the child's relation to the mother's look. For Eidelsztein, the captivating look cannot be reduced to literal optics. It is structured by desire and thus by the Symbolic. Explaining it through a mirror alone conceals the very symbolic determination at issue.

### Five topological consequences

Eidelsztein then gives five reasons topology is more adequate to Lacanian structure.

First, topology is indifferent to shape. Stretching, folding or deforming a surface can change appearance without changing structure. Clinically, this allows a distinction between clinical form and clinical structure. An obsessional-looking presentation can conceal a hysterical structure. Appearance is therefore not determinant.

Second, topology does not privilege measurable distance or size. Eidelsztein links this to psychoanalytic time and space. A subjective instant can have greater weight than years, and geographical separation does not necessarily produce psychic separation. What matters is structural relation, not metric magnitude.

Third, topology reworks the inside/outside opposition. The unconscious can be at once received from the Other and be the subject's most intimate dimension. Ordinary individualism assumes a body separated from an exterior world, but the analytic experience itself requires a relation in which what is most internal is not simply enclosed inside the organism.

Fourth, topology transforms the Cartesian opposition between extended object and non-extended thought. Lacan's object a and the subject cannot be understood as ordinary three-dimensional things. Topological surfaces make available two-dimensional objects whose structural properties do not depend on volume. Eidelsztein uses this to oppose Lacan's object a to any literal three-dimensional satisfaction-object that one could simply locate in empirical reality.

Fifth, topology works with invariants. As shape, distance and ordinary appearance fall away, structural properties remain. Eidelsztein gives "the unconscious is structured like a language" as an example: despite the case-by-case singularity of analytic practice, an invariant structure can still be claimed. This is how he connects structural universality to the psychoanalytic clinic of singular cases.

### Letter, signifier and the graph as a reading device

After establishing the topological orientation, Eidelsztein makes a second historical claim: the graph of desire marks the first systematic entrance of the letter into Lacanian psychoanalysis. He sketches a trajectory from "The Purloined Letter" through "The Instance of the Letter in the Unconscious" to "The Subversion of the Subject". The point is not that Lacan abandons the signifier, but that the graph becomes an instrument for differentiating the signifier from the letter.

Eidelsztein's decisive contrast is that the signifier is listened to whereas the letter is read. He extends this contrast to analytic practice: the analyst is not simply a listener to meanings but a reader of a structure. Lacan's own notation, such as S1 and S2, already stages the issue because the word "signifier" is replaced by a written letter and subscript. The transmission of the theory therefore performs the very distinction it is meant to teach.

A schematic form of the graph provides Eidelsztein with a concrete example. Some positions are occupied by written formulas or letters, while the lateral vectors are labelled with words such as *jouissance*, "signifier", "voice" and "castration". This difference between lettered positions and words on vectors is treated as significant rather than accidental.

[FIGURE: Schema 3, reduced graph with lateral vectors]

Description: four circular vertices form two vertically aligned pairs. The lower row contains `s(A)` on the left and `A` on the right. The upper left contains `S(Ⱥ)` and the upper right contains the drive formula as printed. Curved and horizontal directed edges connect the vertices. Lateral arrows are labelled Jouissance, Signifier, Voice and Castration.
Labels visible in source: `S(Ⱥ)`, drive formula, `s(A)`, `A`, Jouissance, Signifier, Voice, Castration.

Fidelity note: barred-A and the drive formula are visually checked; parsed text corrupts both.

Eidelsztein then advances a deliberately controversial thesis: the graph of desire introduces object a even though object a is not explicitly written as such in the graph. The `a` in `i(a)` belongs to the image of the other, and the `a` in the fantasy formula is not simply a label for the later object-cause in isolation. His stronger claim is structural: the graph itself has the structure of object a. This is why he refuses a purely chronological objection based on the date when Lacan formally named object a.

He also asks why a diagram containing many functions is nevertheless called the *graph of desire*. His provisional answer is that desire is one term among several, but the graph's structure is what makes the different functions mutually intelligible. The answer will emerge only through the progressive construction.

### Euler, Königsberg and the move from map to graph

To demonstrate what a graph is, Eidelsztein turns to Euler's analysis of the seven bridges of Königsberg. The familiar problem asks whether a person can cross each bridge exactly once and return to the starting point. Euler solves it by abandoning the geographical map and transforming the problem into vertices and edges. Shape, size and actual distance no longer matter. What matters is the pattern of connections.

[FIGURE: Schema 4, geographical map of the Koenigsberg bridges]
Source location: printed p. 11 / PDF p. 17
Type: topographic map used before graph-theory abstraction
Description: two elongated river islands and the two river margins are connected by seven bridges. The drawing still preserves geography, relative position and visible bridge shape.
Labels visible in source: no mathematical vertex labels; the bridges and land masses are shown pictorially.
Directional structure: none; this is the representational map that will be transformed into a graph.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: supplies the contrast required by Euler's operation. The next schema discards geographical resemblance and preserves only connectivity.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 17.

[FIGURE: Schema 5, Königsberg graph]

Labels visible in source: Island, Margin of the river, edges 1-7.
Directional structure: undirected.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: the graph demonstrates that topology begins by discarding representational resemblance and retaining only relations of connectivity.
Fidelity note: visually checked.

This transformation is crucial for his psychoanalytic use of graphs. A riverbank can become a point because its empirical extent is irrelevant once the problem is formalized. The same logic will be required for a non-imaginary representation of the subject.

### Graph invariants and the problem of the subject

Eidelsztein introduces a simple "school graph" to explain degree, traversability and the difference between a crossing of lines and a true vertex. A graph is defined as a tripartite structure consisting of a set of vertices, a set of edges and a relation assigning each edge to a pair of vertices. An overlapping pair of edges is not automatically a vertex. This elementary point is later important for distinguishing structural intersections from merely visual crossings in Lacanian diagrams.

The school graph can be traversed completely without repeating an edge only if one starts and finishes at the appropriate odd-degree vertices. The example prepares the formalization of invariants that persist independently of the way the graph is drawn.

[FIGURE: Schema 6, "school graph"]
Source location: printed pp. 13-14 / PDF pp. 19-20
Type: mathematical graph
Description: rectangle-like graph with diagonals and a triangular extension; the diagonal crossing is a false intersection rather than a vertex.
Labels visible in source: traversal numbers/ordering around edges.
Directional structure: undirected; traversal sequence is supplied in the discussion.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: distinguishes graph structure from pictorial appearance and introduces vertex degree and traversability.
Fidelity note: inspected from source text and rendered layout.

The chapter ends by returning to Freud's formula *Wo Es war, soll Ich werden*. Eidelsztein asks why Lacan translates *Ich* as "subject" rather than "ego". His answer comes from Freud's 1895 *Project for a Scientific Psychology*, where Freud asks the reader to picture the ego as a network of cathected neurons. For Eidelsztein, this first Freudian ego is not the unified narcissistic ego. It is a network, and therefore structurally a graph.

[FIGURE: Schema 7, Freud's network of cathected neurons]
Source location: printed p. 15 / PDF p. 21
Type: network schema
Description: Freud's diagram of interconnected neurons, with quantity entering the network and multiple labelled nodes/paths.
Labels visible in source: Q, a, b and Greek-letter node labels.
Directional structure: arrows indicate the movement/diversion of quantity through the network.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: supports the claim that Lacan can read Freud's *Ich* in this context as the subject insofar as the ego in question is a network of representations/signifiers rather than the later narcissistic unity.
Fidelity note: visually checked at source location.

Eidelsztein organizes the result into a historical sequence: Freud's first "introduction of the ego" as network, the 1914 introduction of the narcissistic ego as libidinal object, and Lacan's introduction of the big Other. Subject, ego and Other must therefore be kept distinct. The graph is not an optional illustration added after the theory; it is the formal structure that makes the distinction possible.

### Sources used

- Alfredo Eidelsztein, *The Graph of Desire: Using the Work of Jacques Lacan*, Chapter 1, printed pp. 1-18, project PDF pp. 7-24.

### Object a as unknown and the three dimensions of the problem

Eidelsztein begins with the algebraic character of object a. The letter functions like an unknown variable: it names something that cannot simply be stated by attaching a descriptive attribute. He proposes three analytic cuts into the problem, while stressing that they remain interdependent: a spatial dimension, a temporal dimension and a logical dimension.

The graph of desire is especially suited to the spatial dimension. Eidelsztein reformulates the Cartesian pair *res cogitans/res extensa* as signifying chain/body and asks how object a is localized in relation to both. The temporal dimension appears through Lacan's statement that the only true object a is the child, which Eidelsztein treats as introducing a temporally defined status rather than an empirical object-class. The logical dimension appears through the Freudian inability of the unconscious to inscribe ordinary truth-values and through Lacan's later use of modal logic, in which object a is approached from the side of the impossible.

To formalize the spatial issue he recalls the graph definition `G = (V, E, relation)`: vertices, edges and the relation that links edges to pairs of vertices. The odd-looking open-ended edges of the graph of desire immediately become a technical problem, because a mathematical edge should connect vertices rather than emerge from or disappear into nowhere.

### The 1-2-3 net and the signifying chain

Eidelsztein then turns to Lacan's 1-2-3 net from the seminar on "The Purloined Letter". The net formalizes the transition from chance sequences of plus and minus signs to a diachronic series of signifying terms. It is therefore a graph of a signifying chain.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, the 1-2-3 net]
Source location: printed p. 21 / PDF p. 27
Type: directed graph
Description: four vertices represent the positions called 1, 2, 2 and 3; loops and directed edges connect them according to the admissible transitions.
Labels visible in source: 1, 2, 2, 3.
Directional structure: directed; loops occur at terminal positions.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: shows that a signifying sequence can require more structural positions than its apparent numerical labels suggest and supplies the graph-theoretical vocabulary for the rest of the book.
Fidelity note: source text and rendered page checked.

He defines loop, walk, chain, connectivity and orientation. A loop begins and ends at the same vertex. A walk is a sequence of incident edges. A chain, in the strict graph-theory sense he introduces, does not repeat vertices. Connectivity means that one vertex of a component can be reached from another. Orientation distinguishes directed from undirected graphs.

These terms matter because connectivity in graph theory plays a role analogous to continuity in topology. A graph may consist of disconnected components even when ordinary visual intuition encourages one to treat separate drawings as separate graphs. Conversely, a visual crossing need not constitute a vertex. The structure is relational rather than pictorial.

[FIGURE: Schema 2, connected and disconnected graph components]
Source location: printed p. 22 / PDF p. 28
Type: elementary graph-theory examples
Description: at left, three vertices form a closed triangular component; at right, two vertices are joined by a single edge. The two drawings are spatially separate and have no connecting edge.
Labels visible in source: none.
Directional structure: undirected.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: clarifies connectivity and component structure. A graph can contain disconnected components, so visual proximity or separation does not by itself decide structural continuity.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 28.

Eidelsztein highlights a terminological puzzle: Lacan calls the 1-2-3 construction a "net" and the graph of desire a "graph", even though both can be directed. He does not force a premature answer. The unresolved discrepancy becomes part of the larger question of how Lacan uses mathematical vocabulary for psychoanalytic purposes rather than simply importing it unchanged.

The chapter then moves from connectivity to continuity. Two surfaces are topologically equivalent if they can be put into a one-to-one correspondence without cutting or gluing. This allows Eidelsztein to connect graph theory to psychoanalytic problems of continuity and discontinuity, especially those concerning the subject and object a.

### Invariants, vertex degree and the dimensionality of the subject

Eidelsztein uses graph invariants to answer a central problem of structural psychoanalysis: how can there be principles valid across cases if analytic work insists on singularity? Graphs can vary indefinitely in their drawings while still obeying invariant laws. For him, this provides a formal analogy for the coexistence of case-by-case clinical work and structural properties.

He introduces vertex degree and traversability. The Königsberg graph has four vertices of odd degree, which explains why its seven bridges cannot be traversed exactly once in a closed circuit. The school graph can be traversed from one odd-degree vertex to the other. From such examples he derives the invariant that a graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices and explains the conditions under which all edges can be traversed without repetition.

[FIGURE: Schema 3, vertex degrees and the even-number invariant]
Source location: printed p. 26 / PDF p. 32
Type: mathematical graph
Description: four vertices form a triangular-left / doubled-edge-right configuration. Three vertices are marked degree 3 and the central-right vertex degree 5.
Labels visible in source: 3, 3, 5, 3.
Directional structure: undirected.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: makes visible the invariant that the number of odd-degree vertices is even and supports the discussion of traversability independent of the drawing's shape.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 32.

A further invariant is decisive: every graph can be realized without crossings in three-dimensional space, while only planar graphs can be realized without crossings on a two-dimensional plane or sphere. The familiar puzzle of connecting three houses to three utilities without crossings illustrates why some graphs require three-dimensional realization.

[FIGURE: Schemas 4-6, non-planarity and the one-dimensional comb]
Source location: printed pp. 28-29 / PDF pp. 34-35
Type: graph-theory and Freudian-schema comparison
Description: Schema 4 connects three houses `A`, `B`, `C` to three utility vertices `1`, `2`, `3`, with one connection displaced out of the plane to show the need for a third dimension. Schema 5 renders Freud's comb as a left-to-right chain of vertices and arrows. Schema 6 gives an equivalent comb-like horizontal line with vertical teeth and a single left-to-right direction.
Labels visible in source: `A`, `B`, `C`, `1`, `2`, `3`; the comb schemas have no substantive vertex labels.
Directional structure: Schema 4 is a non-planar connection problem; Schemas 5-6 are one-directional.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: distinguishes the dimensional problem of a non-planar graph from the one-dimensionality of Freud's comb schema and prepares his claim that the psychoanalytic subject requires a two-dimensional topological structure.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF pp. 34-35.

This raises a problem for the graph of desire. Lacan's subject is two-dimensional in the topological sense, yet the graph of desire is non-planar. Eidelsztein therefore begins to oppose ordinary spherical individuality to toric or non-spherical topology. The ordinary individual is conceived as indivisible inside and sharply divided from the external world. The Lacanian subject, by contrast, is internally divided in a way that cannot be represented by an inside/outside sphere.

### Freud's schemata and the two-dimensional signifying chain

Eidelsztein contrasts Freud's neural network with the "comb schema" of *The Interpretation of Dreams*. The comb schema is fundamentally one-dimensional: it lays out a direction from left to right and invites a linear conception of psychic processing. The neural net is two-dimensional and therefore better suited, in his reading, to the structure Lacan later calls the subject.

This distinction allows him to criticize simplistic readings of S1 and S2 as if one signifier merely followed another along a line. Neither mathematical graph-theory chains nor Saussurean linearity is sufficient to capture Lacan's signifying chain because repetition, the other scene and topological embedding cannot be reduced to a one-dimensional sequence.

Eidelsztein takes seriously Lacan's statement that the signifying chain requires a topological substratum. The famous formulation of rings in one necklace being linked to a ring in another necklace is read topologically: the "rings" are not beads on an ordinary chain but tori whose relation is two-dimensional. The signifying chain is therefore not adequately represented by linear succession.

This is also why Eidelsztein defends Lacan's translation of *Wo Es war, soll Ich werden* as "Where it was, there the subject shall be". The relevant *Ich* is, in his reading, the network-ego of Freud's *Project*, not the narcissistic ego of unity.

[FIGURE: Schemas 7-9, from open graph to closed topological circuit]
Source location: printed pp. 31-32 / PDF pp. 37-38
Type: successive reconstructions of the graph of desire
Description: Schema 7 shows the familiar four principal vertices with several edges ending in open arrowheads outside the figure. Schema 8 closes those apparently loose edges with large outer return arcs. Schema 9 gives an alternative closure in which outer and inner circuits are nested as one continuous directed structure.
Labels visible in source: the diagrams are largely unlabeled at this stage; direction is carried by arrowheads and open triangular endpoints.
Directional structure: directed; the later two schemas convert apparently free edges into return circuits.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: demonstrates that the graph should not be read as literally containing edges that originate from nowhere or disappear into nowhere. The closure prepares the interior-eight solution and a continuous account of subjective division.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF pp. 37-38.

### Continuous division and the interior eight

Eidelsztein returns to the open edges of the graph of desire and proposes that they should be read as forming an "interior eight". He contrasts this with a discontinuous solution in which upper and lower parts would remain separate.

The theoretical stake is the Freudian splitting of the ego. The narcissistic ego cannot be the divided term because its defining property is unity. The divided term is the network-like subject. The division relevant to psychoanalysis must also be continuous, not the crude division of one unit into two disconnected pieces. Eidelsztein links this to Freud's *Negation*, where affirmation and negation can imply one another, and to the pulsating unconscious of Seminar XI, which opens and closes while maintaining one boundary.

[FIGURE: Schema 10, discontinuous division versus one-boundary division]
Source location: printed p. 33 / PDF p. 39
Type: topological comparison
Description: the left drawing places a dark inner disk inside a surrounding circle and marks the result as having two boundaries. The right drawing folds one loop into another continuous outline and marks it as having one boundary.
Labels visible in source: `2 boundaries`, `1 boundary`.
Directional structure: not directional; the contrast concerns boundary topology.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: separates ordinary division into two bounded pieces from the continuous division required for the split subject. The latter is the logic developed through the interior eight.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 39.

[FIGURE: Schema 11, graph folded as an interior eight]
Source location: printed p. 34 / PDF p. 40
Type: topological reconstruction of graph of desire
Description: the same four principal vertices and lateral functions as the reduced graph are linked so that upper and lower circuits form a continuous figure rather than two disconnected floors.
Labels visible in source: `S(Ⱥ)`, drive formula, `s(A)`, `A`, Jouissance, Signifier, Voice, Castration.
Directional structure: directed edges form two lobes of one continuous circuit.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: supplies a continuous model of subjective division and keeps signifier/castration and voice/jouissance in structural relation rather than isolating them on separate levels.
Fidelity note: source notation visually checked where extraction was corrupt.

The interior eight solves several conceptual tensions. Voice is an object of jouissance, so a discontinuous model that separates voice from jouissance is unsatisfactory. Castration arises through the signifier, so it too must remain structurally continuous with the signifying dimension. The interior eight permits differentiation without disconnection.

Eidelsztein then opposes spherical and toric conceptions of the subject. Freud's ovum schema from *The Ego and the Id* exemplifies the spherical model: an individual with an inside, an outside and a surface. The sphere supports the culturally familiar ideal of a self-contained individual. Lacanian topology, by contrast, requires a surface on which an internal division can coexist with continuity.

[FIGURE: Schema 12, Freud's second topography as an ovum]

Labels visible in source: `P-Cc`, `Precc`, `Ego`, `Id`, `Repressed`, and the acoustic-system label.
Directional structure: spatial/topographic rather than directed.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: exemplifies the spherical or container-contained model that Eidelsztein opposes to Lacanian topological surfaces. It makes the inside/outside assumptions of an individual-as-ovum visible.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 42.

### Sphere, torus, cut and the hole

Eidelsztein deepens the contrast by recalling the spherical ideal in Western thought, including Aristophanes' myth in Plato's *Symposium*, where original spherical beings are split and seek reunion. The sphere thus carries an old imaginary of completeness and lost unity. The psychoanalytic subject must be represented otherwise.

He introduces the Jordan curve theorem as a practical way to distinguish sphere and torus. Any simple closed curve on a sphere divides the surface into two regions. On a torus this is not always true. A closed cut can open the torus into a cylinder without dividing it into two pieces, and another cut can open the cylinder again while preserving one connected surface.

[FIGURE: Schemas 13-16, cuts on sphere and torus]
Source location: printed pp. 39-40 / PDF pp. 45-46
Type: topological surface diagrams
Description: a Jordan closed curve is shown dividing a spherical surface, followed by two distinct non-separating cuts on a torus and their transformations into cylinder-like/open surfaces.
Labels visible in source: none beyond schema numbers.
Directional structure: cuts rather than arrows organize the figures.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: demonstrates that structural differences are revealed by the right cut, not by visual shape alone, and prepares the identification of object a with an irreducible hole/border relation.
Fidelity note: visually checked from rendered source pages.

This leads to knot theory and to the idea that closed lines on surfaces can be treated as graphs. A cut can reveal a topological invariant that ordinary viewing conceals. Eidelsztein insists that some cuts reveal structure while others hide it, and he explicitly links this to analytic technique. A session ended by the clock is his example of a false cut because it is imposed externally and does not function as a subjective act. A psychoanalytic cut, by contrast, should reveal structure.

He compares four paths around or across a hole. Paths that can be contracted to a point do not establish a structural hole. Paths that cannot be reduced to a point do. The difference between two non-reducible paths concerns whether the cut actually exposes the hole or visually disguises it.

[FIGURE: Schema 17, four paths A-D around a hole]
Source location: printed p. 41 / PDF p. 47
Type: topological path comparison
Description: four line configurations marked A, B, C and D. A and B are reducible to a point; C and D retain a non-reducible relation to a hole, with C displaying the cut more directly than D.
Labels visible in source: A, B, C, D.
Directional structure: path topology rather than directional arrows.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: distinguishes reducible paths from paths whose topology reveals an irreducible hole and differentiates a structure-revealing cut from a false cut.
Fidelity note: visually checked.

The decisive conclusion is that the open, non-circular construction of the graph of desire should be read as an interior eight. The hole is not the apparent center of one lobe. It is the impossible relation between the two repeated circuits, the space whose bordering cannot be collapsed into one closed circle. This irreducible hole is, for Eidelsztein, the spatial dimension of object a and the fundamental structure of the graph itself.

The chapter therefore transforms object a from a thing imagined inside a subject into a structural effect of topology: an irreducible hole produced and revealed by the right cut. Later chapters on fantasy and drive will return to this spatial definition and articulate it with the formulas of the graph.

### Language as a doubled structure

Eidelsztein makes "The Subversion of the Subject" the main reference for the rest of the course and begins from two Lacanian propositions: the unconscious is structured like a language, and the unconscious is a signifying chain that repeats on another scene and interferes in the breaks of effective discourse. The graph of desire is meant to formalize these propositions rather than merely illustrate them.

He reconstructs the linguistic background in two stages. Saussure supplies the lower or inaugural level of modern linguistics: the linguistic sign combines signifier and signified into one psychic entity, while the two terms remain distinct. Eidelsztein stresses the bar separating them because Lacan will make the cut between signifier and signified a privileged place for locating the analytic subject.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, Saussurean sign]
Source location: printed p. 46 / PDF p. 52
Type: linguistic schema
Description: an ellipse contains signified above signifier, separated by a horizontal bar with reciprocal arrows indicating their association.
Labels visible in source: Signified, Signifier.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: establishes the structural two-sidedness of the sign and prepares Lacan's emphasis on the bar/cut.
Fidelity note: visually checked.

Jakobson supplies what Eidelsztein calls, following Lacan, the culminating point of modern linguistics. Code and message can each be used or mentioned and can refer to themselves or to the other. This yields four doubled relations: message/message, code/code, message/code and code/message. Quoted discourse, proper names, metalinguistic explanation and shifters instantiate these relations.

Eidelsztein converts Jakobson's fourfold theory into a graph with two vertices and four edges, two of which are loops. The important point is not the drawing but the doubling of duplicities. Language is already more complex than a simple sender-receiver line.

[FIGURE: Schema 2, graph of code-message relations]
Source location: printed p. 50 / PDF p. 56
Type: directed graph of linguistic relations
Description: two principal vertices corresponding to code and message are joined by cross-relations and each has a self-referential loop.
Labels visible in source: code/message relations as described in the text.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: graphically formalizes Jakobson's four double structures and prepares the idea that subjective division cannot be reduced to two separate egos.
Fidelity note: rendered page checked.

Shifters are especially important because their reference cannot be established from the code alone. Their value depends on the current message. The first-person pronoun is only one example. Tense, reported discourse and other grammatical forms can also shift between statement and enunciation. Eidelsztein uses Jakobson to establish a structural difference between the narrated event and the event of speaking, and between participants in what is narrated and participants in the speech event.

### Why the subject of the unconscious is not the grammatical "I"

Lacan's question is whether, if the unconscious is structured like a language, the subject of the unconscious can simply be identified with the linguistic subject marked by the shifter *je*. Eidelsztein's answer, following Lacan, is no. The shifter designates the subject of enunciation but does not signify what that subject is. Moreover, the signifier of the enunciating subject may be absent from the statement, and many linguistic markers can occupy its place.

This is why Eidelsztein rejects the common reduction of subjective division to the French opposition *moi/je*. That distinction belongs to the grammar of French; it does not by itself formalize the Freudian subject. Lacan's barred subject is needed because the analytic subject cannot be fixed to a grammatical pronoun.

Lacan's discussion of the French expletive *ne* provides a better example. The *ne* can be syntactically necessary while carrying no ordinary negative meaning. Eidelsztein treats this as a mark in the language-code of a subject that is not reducible to semantic content. Yet he immediately distinguishes this code-level mark from analytic practice, where the analyst seeks the subject in a singular discourse, that is, in the message rather than merely in the language-system.

### The subject of the interval

Eidelsztein emphasizes that the analytic subject can speak without knowing that it speaks. Symptoms are decisive examples: something is said where the person does not recognize a saying at all. The unconscious is therefore not simply a second inner speaker who means the opposite of the conscious ego.

He develops Lacan's formulation of the *inter-said* as the *intra-said* of a between-two-subjects. The message cannot be securely owned by a sender or receiver; it emerges in the interval between positions. As the determining signifier becomes purer, the subject becomes more eclipsed because the subject falls between one signifier and another. Elision, slips and jokes reveal presence through absence rather than through full self-presence.

This allows Eidelsztein to reread the Fort-Da game. Against a simple reading in terms of displeasure at absence, he argues that the symbolic structure makes absence a way of producing presence. Elision is not merely a lack of representation; it is a structural mode of presence.

Lacan's statement that the subject is verified by the cut in the signifying chain leads Eidelsztein to propose the term "subject of the interval". The subject is neither one signifier nor the other but what is localized in the break between them. This immediately requires a triadic rather than dual conceptual device: need-demand-desire.

### Demand alienates need

Eidelsztein turns to "The Signification of the Phallus" to reconstruct the triad. Because the human being speaks, need is diverted by being subjected to demand. The alienation does not arise primarily from biological helplessness or real dependence; it arises from signifying form and from the fact that the subject's message comes from the locus of the Other.

Demand therefore produces an inversion. What had appeared as the subject's own need returns from the Other. Eidelsztein distinguishes this from another inversion to be studied later, in which the subject receives its own message from the Other in inverted form.

The portion of need that cannot be articulated in demand is treated as primal repression. It does not simply return as another need. It gives rise to desire. This allows Eidelsztein to replace a simple frustration model with the structural logic of demand: demand is not exhausted by the request for an object that would satisfy a biological need.

Demand addresses the presence or absence of the Other. The maternal function is therefore not defined biologically but as the place in which the Other of language is incarnated for the child. The Other acquires power because it can give or withhold not merely an object but its presence.

[FIGURE: Schema 3, need-demand-desire]
Source location: printed p. 60 / PDF p. 66
Type: conceptual sequence
Description: Need appears on the left, Demand in the middle and Desire on the right. The border between need and demand is labelled "Within" (*au deçà*), and the border between demand and desire "Beyond" (*au-delà*).
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: marks demand as the torsional operation through which need is alienated and desire emerges beyond demand.
Fidelity note: visually checked.

The Other of demand is initially omnipotent because there is no internal limit to the place from which language and presence are bestowed. Eidelsztein's clinical example is the small child's rage when the mother fails to understand speech: what is shaken is not simply the child's omnipotence but the presumed omnipotence of the Other who was thought to possess the mother tongue.

### Desire as remainder and absolute condition

Demand abolishes the species-specific particularity of need by transforming whatever could satisfy the need into a proof of love. Eidelsztein follows Lacan's use of *Aufhebung*: the particularity of need is cancelled but also preserved in transformed form. The particular object that would satisfy the species is lost, while the demand for love becomes unconditional.

What is abolished at the level of species reappears beyond demand as the subject's particularity. Eidelsztein treats this as the decisive passage to desire. Desire is neither appetite for satisfaction nor demand for love. It is the difference produced when need is subtracted from demand, the residue of their split.

This is the bridge to object a. If desire is a remainder, then the later account of object a as remainder is structurally prepared here. The particularity lost from need returns not as a biological object but as the singular, absolute condition that organizes the subject's desire.

Eidelsztein differentiates the unconditional character of demand from the absolute condition of desire. Unconditional demand establishes the omnipotence of the Other; an absolute condition does not. Desire's condition is not a relative request within demand but a structural cause that organizes the subject's position.

The need-demand-desire relation is then given a Möbius-strip structure. Demand is the torsion that transforms the "within" of need into the "beyond" of desire. The apparent two sides belong to one continuous surface.

[FIGURE: Schema 4, emergence of desire beyond demand]
Source location: printed p. 66 / PDF p. 72
Type: partial graph of desire
Description: a horizontal signifying vector from S to S' crosses a vertical/curved circuit at A. The lower end of the circuit is marked with the barred subject, while a simplified vertical version places A between an origin below and desire `d` above.
Labels visible in source: S, S', A, barred subject, d.
Directional structure: the signifying chain proceeds toward S'; the vertical/curved trajectory passes through A toward desire.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: locates desire beyond the Other of demand and presents the graph as a formalization of the triad.
Fidelity note: visually checked.

Eidelsztein uses this structure to explain Lacan's statement that desire is articulated but not articulable. Desire presupposes the articulation of demand in the Other, yet what emerges as residue is precisely what cannot itself be included in the demand. The object a as cause is therefore articulated by the signifying operation while remaining non-articulable as a demanded object.

[FIGURE: Schemas 5 and 6, summary of need-demand-desire and Möbius torsion]
Source location: printed p. 67 / PDF p. 73
Type: conceptual table and topological schema
Description: Schema 5 aligns Need/particular object/species with Demand/Other/proof of love/unconditional character and Desire/object a/particularity/absolute condition. Schema 6 depicts one looping surface with "Within" on one side, "Beyond" on the other and *renversement* at the torsion.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: summarizes the transformations across demand and gives the triad a Möbius rather than linear structure.
Fidelity note: visually checked.

Eidelsztein closes by announcing a later substitution: because "need" is mythical at the level of the analytic clinic, later chapters will increasingly replace it with jouissance. For the moment, however, the triad establishes why the graph is specifically a graph of desire: it formalizes the subject as the interval produced by signifying demand and the remainder that demand cannot recover.

### Desire is articulated but not articulable

Eidelsztein introduces Graph 1 through Lacan's paradoxical formula that desire is articulated precisely because it is not articulable. Desire cannot be reduced to an ineffable universal remainder common to everyone. It is articulated for each subject insofar as it is determined by the Other's demand. The question "What do you want?" arises only against the background of "What are you saying to me?" Desire therefore exceeds demand but is structurally determined by it.

He stresses that the small `d` of desire should not be read as simply indicating that desire belongs to the Imaginary. Rather, desire is an effect of the Symbolic which cannot be fully reabsorbed into the Symbolic order. It remains what demand cannot recapture.

Graph 1 is not a clinical structure that exists independently in a patient. Eidelsztein treats Graphs 1, 2 and 3 as didactic cuts in the complete graph. They isolate moments of a deductive construction so that a fundamentally synchronous structure can be taught diachronically.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, first drawing of Graph 1]
Source location: printed p. 72 / PDF p. 77
Type: Graph 1, elementary cell
Description: a horizontal vector runs from `S` at the left toward `S'` at the right. A second curved trajectory crosses it twice, loops above it and descends to two lower endpoints, one marked by the barred-subject position and the other by an open triangular endpoint.
Labels visible in source: `S`, `S'`, barred-subject position.
Directional structure: the horizontal vector advances left-to-right while the second vector loops retroactively through the two crossing points.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: introduces the elementary cell before its crossing points are given their developed names, allowing anticipation and retroaction to be derived before the later graph notation is imposed.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 77.

### The elementary cell and point de capiton

Lacan calls Graph 1 the graph's "elementary cell". Eidelsztein reads it through the point de capiton, the quilting point, which stops the otherwise indefinite sliding of signification. He carefully distinguishes this from the simplistic idea that a signifier always leads to another signifier. What indefinitely slides is signification. A quilting point can temporarily close that movement.

The upholstery metaphor matters because a quilting point is not just a final dot. It is a knot binding two layers together and distributing tension through a continuous bow. Eidelsztein uses this to insist that punctuation in analysis is structural and relational. Merely stopping a session by the clock does not constitute an analytic cut.

The Other has the power to punctuate discourse. This is why the subject receives its own message from the Other: not because someone else literally speaks the subject's words, but because the Other's punctuation determines what those words come to signify. Yet not every punctuation made by another person counts as an interpretation.

### Diachrony: anticipation and retroaction

The diachronic function of the quilting point involves two temporal directions. The last term retroactively seals or loops the sentence's signification, while earlier terms anticipate what can follow. Eidelsztein is attentive to Lacan's verb *boucler*: the phrase closes like a curl or loop, not simply like a door.

Retroaction therefore coexists with anticipation. The first signifying choice already restricts what can come later, while the last term retroactively fixes what preceded it. Eidelsztein links this to the later notation of S1: once a master signifier is chosen, not just anything can follow.

The resulting temporality is non-metric. It is structured by scansion, anticipation and retroaction rather than by measurable duration.

<!--
CHAPTER: 04
PDF_PAGES: 083-088

### Synchrony, metaphor and the birth of the signifier

For the synchronic dimension Eidelsztein follows Lacan's example: "the dog goes miaow, the cat goes woof-woof". When the child's word breaks the natural relation between thing and cry, the cry ceases to function merely as a sign and becomes a signifier. The act is metaphorical because one sign is substituted for another and the previously natural relation is displaced.

This transformation also affects reality. Once signs are treated as signifiers, reality is no longer simply represented by natural signs. It becomes organized by the "sophistics of signification", in which truth has the structure of an argument that can simultaneously contain truth and falsity. Eidelsztein uses Dora and the Rat Man as examples: an analytic proposition may be structurally true without being literally exact in the ordinary empirical sense.

The child's cry undergoes the same transformation. Once the mother interprets it as a signifier rather than a fixed sign of a need, it becomes a call. Both the thing and the cry are denaturalized. Eidelsztein connects this to Lacan's discussion of insult and attribution: to call someone "this" or "that" is already to impose a signifying attribute that damages any supposed natural being. Symbolic thought begins through this substitution.

Synchrony and diachrony are thus already present in the elementary cell. Diachrony gives anticipation and retroaction. Synchrony gives attribution, metaphor and the cut through which a subject is constituted in the Symbolic.

### Place and time become localization and scansion

Eidelsztein then translates ordinary spatial and temporal notions into topological ones. The Other is a locus, not an empirical space. Its position is structural, without metric dimensions. Likewise, the moment of the message is a rhythm or scansion rather than a measurable duration.

This provides the formal basis for variable-length sessions. The analytic question is not simply how many minutes have passed, but when a scansion occurs, whether it comes too soon or too late, or whether it fails to occur at all. Space becomes localization and time becomes scansion.

Lacan's question whether the graph requires a four-cornered topology is decisive. A merely dual relation between subject and Other cannot account for the unconscious. The quilting point itself already suggests a two-by-two linking structure. The complete graph will need four places.

### The elementary cell as repetition, not enclosure

Eidelsztein rejects the biological reading of "cell" as a unit enclosed by a membrane. Such a model would reinstall an inside/outside opposition between subject and Other. He prefers the sense of cell as a repetitive element. The elementary cell repeats a circuit.

If the graph remained only the circular movement from the Other to signification and back again, it would be an "infernal circuit of demand". Eidelsztein uses Dante's Inferno as an image of circular demand: complaint, lament and supplication circulate endlessly with no exit. The circuit is made of signifiers but is, by itself, insufficient to produce certainty or an act.

The exit from this infernal circle must therefore lie beyond demand, in desire. An act capable of producing certainty cannot be generated from the circularity of demand alone.

### Psychosis, demand and the absence of a beyond

This provides Eidelsztein with a structural distinction between neurosis and psychosis. The psychotic subject is still a subject of language. There is still an Other, and code/message structures, circularity and overlapping continue to operate. Psychosis is not the absence of language or the absence of signifiers.

The decisive difference is whether a beyond of demand operates. In psychosis, as Eidelsztein reads Lacan here, the subject remains trapped in the demand circuit. The subject of language is produced by articulation among at least two signifiers, but a distinct field of desire does not open beyond that circuit in the same way.

[FIGURE: Schema 3, Graph 1 as an `S1`-`S2` articulation]
