Description: the two crossing points are now circular vertices labeled `S1` and `S2`; an upper retroactive arc returns from `S2` toward `S1`, while the lower branches descend to the barred-subject position and the open endpoint.
Labels visible in source: `S1`, `S2`, barred-subject position.
Directional structure: a left-to-right signifying chain crossed by a retroactive return.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: makes explicit that the subject of language is produced through at least two signifiers. The schema supports the subsequent contrast between neurotic and psychotic relations to the circuit rather than depicting psychosis as absence of language.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 90.

Eidelsztein closes with Lacan's formulation that jouissance can only be said "between the lines" for the subject of the Law. He insists on the etymological force of *inter-dict*: what is structurally decisive is the "between". The Law is not simply an external prohibition that later creates an interval; the interval itself grounds the Law. This prepares a clinic that cannot be reduced to paternal prohibition alone and makes the four-cornered topology necessary for the next stages of the graph.

## Chapter 5 - Questions and answers: The impossible - neurosis and psychosis

<!--
CHAPTER: 05
PDF_PAGES: 093-100

### From need-demand-desire to jouissance-demand-desire

Chapter 5 begins as a question-and-answer session. Eidelsztein first clarifies the difference between demand's "unconditional" character and desire as "absolute condition". These terms specify relations within the triad rather than properties that can be understood in isolation. Demand interrupts the continuity between need and desire, and each of the two borders has a different logic.

He now qualifies the earlier use of "need". For the speaking being, vital need is already too mythical to serve as a final psychoanalytic category. The course is therefore moving toward the triad jouissance-demand-desire. What survives of necessity is fundamentally logical necessity, not an untouched biological imperative.

The relation between need, demand and desire is nevertheless a genuine triad because what is lost as species-particularity at the level of need returns, transformed, as the subject's singular object-cause. This conservation-through-transformation gives the triad its Möbius structure. The object a is the transformed offspring of what demand makes irrecoverable.

Eidelsztein next addresses why Lacan continues to use diagrams if his teaching moves away from ordinary representation. His answer is not that representation can be abolished. The task is to choose representations whose internal logic better exhibits how saying determines intuition. Topological diagrams are therefore superior not because they escape representation but because they make intuitive form subordinate to structure.

A similar qualification applies to enunciation and the unconscious. At this stage of Lacan's work, Eidelsztein says, they can partly overlap, but the analytic subject is not identical with either the subject of statement or the subject of enunciation. It is localized between them. The interior-eight logic adds repetition to the interval: the neurotic subject requires both a failure of encounter and a return to that failure.

This leads back to object a. Repetition is never exact. Something is lost between an original and its repetition. Object a is localized in this difference, and because repetition presupposes counting or symbolic inscription, the loss is itself a symbolic effect.

### The impossible as structural, not merely difficult

Eidelsztein introduces the mathematical problem of squaring the circle to clarify Lacan's use of impossibility. The question is not whether a solution has simply not yet been found. In mathematics, an impossible construction is one that contradicts the rules of the formal system under which it is posed.

Lacan's question is whether the dual elementary cell can be "squared" into the four-cornered topology required by the complete graph. If the Other were a complete battery that exhaustively contained every signifier and every combinatorial possibility, such a closure might be possible. But the Other relevant to the subject is not complete in this sense.

Eidelsztein uses the transcendental character of pi to show how a finite determination can involve an infinite, non-repeating expansion and thus defeat ordinary intuition. The mathematical examples serve to separate rigorous impossibility from empirical ignorance. A construction can be hard, unknown or technologically unavailable without being impossible. Psychoanalysis needs the stronger, structural sense.

<!--
CHAPTER: 05
PDF_PAGES: 101-105
PRINTED_PAGES: 97-101
STATUS: COMPLETE
-->

### The incomplete Other and the neurosis-psychosis opposition

For Eidelsztein, the impossibility relevant to the graph follows from the incompleteness of the Other. He sharply distinguishes the Other as a *battery* of signifiers from the Other as a *treasure* of signifiers. A battery can be complete in the ordinary sense that all its elements are present. A treasure, by contrast, is constitutively not-all: if it contained absolutely everything of value, the very economy of value would collapse. The subject's relation to the Other depends on this structural incompleteness.

This is why the passage from the dual circuit of Graph 1 to the full four-cornered topology cannot be treated as a simple quantitative addition. The subject is constituted by subtracting itself from the Other and thereby "decompleting" it. The missing term is not a temporary gap waiting to be filled by more knowledge.

Eidelsztein then uses Lacan's "Question Preliminary" to formulate a quaternary Oedipal structure. The mother, father and their relation do not exhaust the topology. The subject as fourth term is foreclosed from the system as a directly representable element and only enters the play of signifiers through what the structure makes signify.

On this basis Eidelsztein rejects the simple opposition "repression = neurosis / foreclosure = psychosis". Both structures involve a lack, but the locus of foreclosure differs. In psychosis, foreclosure affects the Name-of-the-Father, the signifier of law in the Other. In neurosis, Eidelsztein says, the foreclosed or absent term is the signifier that would represent the subject itself in the Other.

The Name-of-the-Father functions as a quilting point that stabilizes the four-place topology. Where it operates, lack is legalized. Where it is foreclosed, lack is not symbolically legalized and the infernal demand circuit tends toward infinitization rather than bounded interdiction.

This allows Eidelsztein to state a strong structural claim: a neurotic cannot become psychotic, and a psychotic cannot become neurotic, because the difference is not one of degree or difficulty but a different location of structural impossibility. The proposed transformation would be like asking the formal system to violate its own rule.

### Certitude, self-reference and neurotic self-exclusion

Psychosis nevertheless contains a subject, an Other and language. Eidelsztein even provocatively says that, in one respect, there is "more subject" in psychosis because the psychotic subject can have a direct certitude of self-reference. The central clinical index is not ordinary certainty about facts but certainty that the signifier concerns the subject.

Neurosis is characterized in the opposite direction: by self-exclusion from the signifier that would represent the subject. The hysteric and obsessional are two different responses to the same structural nonexistence of a signifier that would finally name the subject. The hysteric sustains the lack; the obsessional attempts to deny or close it.

The chapter ends by redefining impossibility as enabling rather than merely restrictive. The impossible establishes the structural boundary within which possibilities exist. Without such a limit, there would be no determinate field of action or desire.

- Alfredo Eidelsztein, *The Graph of Desire: Using the Work of Jacques Lacan*, Chapter 5, printed pp. 89-101, project PDF pp. 93-105.

## Chapter 6 - Ideal (I) - ego (m) - ideal (i): Graph 2

<!--

### Other, truth and the distinction between symbolic and imaginary deception

Eidelsztein develops Graph 2 through the relation among the ego Ideal, the Ideal ego and the Other. He begins by broadening the function of `A`: the Other is not only the locus of speech but also witness to Truth. Because Lacan treats his concepts as signifiers, the meaning of "Other" changes with the system of relations in which it appears. It is therefore methodologically wrong to demand one fixed dictionary definition independent of context.

This contextual logic is used to distinguish symbolic truth from imaginary pretence. Animals can mislead predators by a false movement, but they cannot "pretend to pretend": they cannot produce a true track in such a way that it will be taken as false. Human speech can do precisely this because truth and lying operate through the signifier and through a third locus, the Other as witness.

Truth therefore does not receive its guarantee from empirical reality. It receives the mark of truth from speech itself and so has a fictional structure. The result is not that truth is arbitrary, but that the truth/lie relation is internally mediated by the signifier. A true statement can function through deception and a false statement can carry truth.

### `I(A)` as the One of the Other

Eidelsztein then turns to the lower-left endpoint of Graph 2, `I(A)`. He resists the obvious reading of the capital `I` merely as the first letter of "Ideal". It can also be read as the Roman numeral one: the One of the Other. The formula isolates one signifier from the Other and treats it as an insignia of the Other's omnipotence.

The "first said" acquires the force of decree, law, aphorism or oracle because a signifier is extracted from the Other and made to stand as One. Eidelsztein sees here the precursor of Lacan's later master-signifier `S1`. The omnipotence of the One must remain obscure: as soon as another signifier is added to explain it, the One is relativized within a signifying articulation and is no longer omnipotent.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, Graph 2 with I(A)]
Source location: printed p. 107 / PDF p. 110
Type: second didactic stage of graph of desire
Description: the elementary lower graph is supplemented by the symbolic ideal `I(A)` at the lower left endpoint, linked into the pathway traversed by the subject.
Labels visible in source: `I(A)` and the lower graph positions.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: localizes the symbolic ideal as the One extracted from the Other and prepares the opposition with the Ideal ego.
Fidelity note: rendered source page checked.

Eidelsztein treats this as a revision of Freud. Freud's ego ideal can be described as cultural and ethical representations and as a factor in repression. Lacan shifts the problem from the content of ideals to the structural elevation of one signifier into One. He also shifts emphasis from the subject's own supposed narcissistic omnipotence to the omnipotence attributed to the Other.

The therapeutic implication follows directly. The problem is not to destroy ideals in general but to undo the isolation of an insignia as absolute One by reinserting it into a chain where it can become `S1` relative to an `S2`.

The comparison with the complete graph clarifies the direction of Graph 2. Eidelsztein asks the reader to contrast the upper-left `S({barA})`, where lack in the Other is inscribed, with the lower-left `I(A)`, where the One of the Other supplies the subject with an ideal point of arrest. The graph therefore places lack and idealization on one pathway rather than treating them as independent topics.

### Alienation, primary identification and retroversion

Eidelsztein describes primary identification as identification with the One of the Other. This identity is necessarily alienating because what appears to give the subject a stable identity comes from the Other. Graph 2 stages this by placing the subject's pathway in relation to both `I(A)` and the image of the other.

[FIGURE: Schema 3, Graph 1 compared with all later graphs]

Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 115.

The passage has a paradoxical temporality. Lacan's term "retroversion" is central for Eidelsztein: the subject becomes at each stage what it "will have been". The future perfect expresses a past that is constituted only from a later position. There is therefore no fully formed subject prior to primary identification. The identification retrospectively produces the earlier moment as the moment from which the subject is said to have emerged.

Eidelsztein adds another formulation of the same problem: the subject is not only between one signifier and another, but can also be written as caught between zero and One. `I(A)` occupies the side of One, while the barred subject marks the zero produced by signifying loss. This is not numerical psychology; it is a way of writing how an ideal can cover the lack opened by signification.

Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 116.

Eidelsztein opposes this to Freud's tendency, especially in the Wolf Man, to search for one originary event. Analytic work should multiply versions rather than force experience toward one original scene. Because every signifying version is one among possible interpretations, the subject's act concerns which version can function as the most truthful in the present configuration.

Self-knowledge is consequently structured by misrecognition. To know oneself through the Other's ideal is also to become more alienated in that ideal. The subject's attempt to find a stable self through the Other is not a route to transparent identity.

### Ideal ego as imaginary response to symbolic alienation

The mirror image offers a second resource. The subject catches an anticipated image of bodily unity and treats it as its own. Eidelsztein stresses that this is not a genuinely self-generated image. It is the image of the other, `i(a)`, and its anticipatory character makes it alienating.

Graph 2 therefore places the subject between two forms of otherness: the symbolic ideal `I(A)` and the imaginary image `i(a)`. Imaginary alienation is not an alternative to symbolic alienation that would free the subject from the Other. It is another mode of dependence on alterity.

The ideal image becomes fixed only because the subject has already halted at a signifier. Eidelsztein links this to Lacan's later notion of petrification: identification with one signifier stops metonymic movement. Without that symbolic halt, images could continue to shift and no single image would become the fixed site of narcissistic capture.

The mother's fascinated gaze in the mirror scene is therefore not sufficient by itself. The image captures because the symbolic ideal has already provided a point of fixation.

<!--

### The ego is transcendent, not immanent

Eidelsztein clarifies Lacan's claim that the ego is not immanent to the subject. "Immanent" would mean that the ego resides within the subject's own nature and is caused by itself. Lacan's ego is instead doubly transcendent: it is determined from beyond its supposed boundaries by the signifier of the Other and by the other's image.

The ego is therefore neither an essence nor an a priori autonomous function. It is an effect of the signifier and the mirror relation. Its central achievement is misrecognition: it conceals the otherness of the causes that constitute it and presents itself as "I am myself".

This misrecognition produces projection. The ego seeks sameness in the environment and treats difference as rivalry or threat. Eidelsztein links this to narcissistic aggressivity and to the projective surface on which images are formed, anticipating the later discussion of fantasy and reality.

[FIGURE: Schemas 5 and 6, imaginary and symbolic circuits of Graph 2]

Labels visible in source: `I(A)`, `i(a)`, `m`, `s(A)`, `A`, subject position.

Fidelity note: rendered source pages checked.

Eidelsztein identifies two characteristic dead ends. The first is the short circuit of petrification at `I(A)`, where the subject adheres to one signifier. The second is the endless metonymy of ego-signification, where the subject moves from one "I am this" to another without reaching a final identity. Both can look like routes toward self-knowledge, but neither opens the field of desire.

The ethical consequence is a "beyond the ideals". This is not a moral rejection of ideals but a structural requirement of treatment. If the subject remains within either symbolic petrification or imaginary-metonymic self-definition, the dialectic of desire cannot proceed. The analytic pass must therefore traverse both idealizing solutions rather than perfect them.

### Graph 3 and the problem of the new

Eidelsztein introduces Graph 3 through a clinical question: how can analysis open something genuinely new rather than reproduce the infernal circle of demand or the metonymic substitutions of ego-identity? He contrasts Freud's account of idealization with sublimation. Idealization heightens the ego's demands and favors repression, while sublimation changes the aim of the drive and offers a way out that is not simply the elevation of the same object.

He reads this opposition as one between sameness and otherness. Idealization remains tied to the same object, enlarged or exalted. Sublimation introduces another route. This prepares Lacan's stronger notion of a pass beyond the impasses of the ideals. The "new" in psychoanalysis is not a new item added to an old series but a change in subjective position.

The beyond of demand now becomes central. Every demand opens a margin that it cannot itself close. That margin is desire. Eidelsztein insists that the fundamental problem is not the subject's own omnipotence but the presumed omnipotence of the Other on which demand depends. The usual fantasy that paternal Law must simply restrain an omnipotent subject reverses the structural order.

Lacan's move, as Eidelsztein presents it, is that desire is autonomous with respect to the paternal Law because Law itself originates in the field opened by desire. The lack is not first introduced by paternal prohibition. Rather, the paternal operation can be inscribed because lack already belongs to the structure.

This is a decisive departure from the neurotic theory that one desires only what is forbidden. To make prohibition the cause of desire is to veil a more fundamental lack. Eidelsztein's example is the "rebel without a cause": the subject who organizes desire around whatever is forbidden in order to avoid confronting the uncaused lack that no prohibition produced.

Graph 3 formalizes the detachment. Desire `d` appears beyond the Other `A`, not on the demand line itself. The graph also places the question `Che vuoi?` between the lines and fantasy at the point that supports or closes the opening created by the question.

### Transitional object, fetish and the difference between emblem and cause

Eidelsztein uses Winnicott's transitional object as the simplest clinical model of detachment from the Other. The crucial feature is its fixed particularity: it must be this bit of cloth, this shard, this object. Such an object inscribes an absolute condition. Yet Lacan, as Eidelsztein reads him, calls it only an emblem of the deeper structure.

The transitional object preserves a signifying function while being an object. It can support a first separation from the Other's demand, but it can also become an emblem of the Other's omnipotence. Eidelsztein places the fetish in the same family of problems: the fetish both acknowledges and disavows lack, stopping at an object that functions as a screen or veil.

The real issue is representation. No signifier directly delivers the thing. The neurotic maneuver of fixing on a privileged object tries to convert an emblem into the thing itself and thereby obscure the structural cause of desire. The object a must therefore be distinguished from the empirical object that carries its emblematic function.

### Two different "of the Other" formulas

A major section is devoted to disentangling two Lacanian formulas often treated as equivalent: "the unconscious is the discourse of the Other" and "man's desire is the desire of the Other". Eidelsztein uses grammar to distinguish objective and subjective genitives.

In the first formula, "of the Other" is read objectively: the unconscious speaks *about* or in relation to the Other. In the second, it is read subjectively: it is as Other that the subject desires. The second formula therefore does not merely mean that the subject wants what the Other wants or wants the Other as an object. It means that the place from which desire occurs is structurally Other.

This distinction explains the opacity of desire. A subject may eventually circumscribe demands, including what is demanded in analysis. What cannot be made transparent in the same way is the place from which desire proceeds. The structure is less "I desire" than "it is desired".

This is also why a fixed object can create the fiction "I desire that". In obsessional formations, Eidelsztein notes, the cause of desire can be reduced to the absolute condition of one object. The subject then experiences determination as personal decisiveness, while the structural cause remains veiled.

### `Che vuoi?` and the analyst's desire

The Other's question returns to the subject in the form `Che vuoi?`, "What do you want?" Eidelsztein reconstructs a sequence of inversions. The subject asks the Other about desire; the Other's answer returns as a question to the subject; the subject then reformulates it as "What do you want from me?" This last form exposes the subject's tendency to place itself as object of the Other's desire.

The function of the question is more important than its biographical content. Children's repeated "why?" offers a pure model: each answer is rejected so the question itself remains operative.

[FIGURE: Schema 2, simplified Graph 3]
Source location: printed p. 139 / PDF p. 141
Type: simplified graph
Description: a reduced version isolates the relation between demand, the Other and the question/desire structure above it.
Labels visible in source: principal graph positions relevant to `Che vuoi?` and desire.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: shows the pure structural function of the question independently of detailed graph content.
Fidelity note: rendered source page checked.

The analytic maneuver follows. The analyst does not simply satisfy demand because satisfaction would close the very margin in which desire can emerge. Frustration of demand produces an object effect, after which the analyst must sustain a desiring position. This is Eidelsztein's route to the "desire of the analyst".

The analysand is therefore not approached only as a desiring subject but also as an object positioned in relation to the analyst's presumed desire. The two poles, desired object and desiring subject, are joined in what Eidelsztein calls the position of the desiring object.

Fantasy is introduced at exactly this point. It is the structural support through which the neurotic can organize the otherwise opaque question of desire. Hence the clinic of neurosis as a clinic of the question becomes, at the same time, a clinic of fantasy.

- Alfredo Eidelsztein, *The Graph of Desire: Using the Work of Jacques Lacan*, Chapter 7, printed pp. 125-141, project PDF pp. 127-143.

## Chapter 8 - Desire and fantasme: A pathway (I) - the symptom

<!--

### Desire and fantasy as a pathway

Eidelsztein opens by refusing to treat either desire or fantasy as an isolated topic. In his reading of Lacan, neither can be taught coherently on its own because Graph 3 introduces desire `d`, the question `Che vuoi?`, and fantasy simultaneously. The relevant object of study is therefore the articulation between desire and fantasy, and that articulation has the form of a pathway. The graph is oriented: its edges have a direction, so it can formalize the "ways" and "defiles" through which a subject moves in the signifier.

He maps the pathway through a sequence of Lacanian texts: "On a Question Preliminary to Any Possible Treatment of Psychosis", "The Direction of the Treatment", "Remark on Daniel Lagache's Report", "Subversion of the Subject", Seminars VIII and X, and "Kant with Sade". Eidelsztein's historical thesis is that fantasy has a more structurally central place in Lacan's clinic of neurosis than unconscious phantasy has in Freud's explicit theory, even though Freud's practice already points in that direction.

The Rat Man supplies the first example. Eidelsztein stresses that the rat torture fantasy was not the patient's symptom proper. The symptom was his "delay in life": the deferral of a decision between two women. Analysis itself risked repeating that delay because the patient had to suspend ordinary life in order to travel to Freud. Freud's admission that therapeutic success prevented him from unraveling the "tissue of phantasy" thread by thread allows Eidelsztein to distinguish symptom relief from the fuller direction of the cure. The tissue metaphor is read as a network or weave. Analytic progress therefore cannot be reduced to symptom elimination; it must reach the fantasy through which desire is sustained.

### Symptom, metaphor and metonymy

On the graph, the symptom is located at `s(A)`, the signified of the Other and an effect of signification. Eidelsztein initially follows the familiar claim that the symptom is a metaphor: a movement from the upper chain, through fantasy, toward `s(A)` can be drawn as a vertical substitution. Yet he immediately argues that the complete graph prevents a purely metaphorical reading. The symptom is crossed by both vertical and horizontal relations and thus has a metonymic as well as a metaphoric slope.

[FIGURE: Completed graph and Schemas 1-3]

Type: graph-of-desire pathway diagrams

Labels visible in source: upper lack-in-the-Other position, fantasy formula, `s(A)`, `A`, lower and upper graph chains; arrows marked "Metaphorical substitution" and "Metonymical combination".
Directional structure: metaphor is represented by movement between the two graph levels; metonymy by movement along the signifying chain.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: prevents the symptom from being reduced to metaphor alone and prepares a structural contrast between hysterical and obsessional symptom formation.
Fidelity note: diagram sequence visually checked against the source; notation normalized only where the symbol is unambiguous.

Eidelsztein associates the more metaphorical structure with hysterical conversion, where one representation can condense opposed terms of a conflict. The obsessional symptom, by contrast, often unfolds metonymically in a sequence of opposed acts, such as removing a stone and then putting it back. He also uses the hysteria and obsession fantasy formulae from Seminar VIII to show that the obsessional formula explicitly contains a serial sequence of objects.

[FIGURE: Schema 4, symptom as articulation with the Other]
Source location: printed p. 148 / PDF p. 149
Type: graph detail
Description: the symptom position is shown not merely as a junction of the two signifying chains but as a vertex whose structure also includes the Other `A`.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: supports the proposition that the symptom is not a private formation detached from language but is constituted in the Other.
Fidelity note: source figure inspected.

### The symptom is "of the Other"

Eidelsztein develops the point through "Question Preliminary". The subject's question is particular, but the material from which it is articulated is received from the Other, especially the fixed rhetorical figures and tropes of a language. Their relative fixity explains both the fixity of symptoms and their decipherability. The analyst can read the symptom because analyst and analysand participate in the same symbolic resources, much as Freud's theory of jokes presupposes a shared linguistic parish.

This leads from the symptom to the problem of the subject's existence. Eidelsztein notes Lacan's correction of an earlier recognition model: the subject cannot be finally recognized by the Other because the subject is what a signifier represents for another signifier and thus falls into the interval between them. Its existence is therefore "ineffable" and appears with stupefaction or surprise when a later signifier retroactively resignifies an earlier one.

The fundamental questions concern sex and life, precisely where common sense expects biology to settle matters. "What is it to be a man or a woman?" and the contingency of being alive become questions only because the signifier has made existence non-self-identical. The subject's question both exposes lack and supplies a support for the subject: where existence vanishes under the signifier, the subject sustains itself in the question "Who am I?" Fantasy now appears as one of the discursive forms through which this question is supported.

### Fantasy is constituted in the Other

Eidelsztein asks whether a fantasy is "particular" to the subject or articulated in the Other. He uses a schema from Seminar X that divides "Other's side" from "my side" and places the relevant terms across that division. His conclusion is deliberately strong: fantasy is located entirely in the Other. A subject cannot resolve anything decisive about fantasy without a device that includes the place of the Other. This is one reason analysis cannot be replaced by solitary introspection.

[FIGURE: Schema 5, Other's side / my side]
Source location: printed p. 151 / PDF p. 152
Type: two-column structural schema
Description: the figure separates an "Other's side" from "My side" and places Lacanian letters on the two sides, including `A` and the object position.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: formalizes the claim that the subject's apparently private question and fantasy are structurally constituted in the Other.
Fidelity note: figure inspected visually; only clearly legible labels are relied upon in the reconstruction.

### Desire beyond demand and the direction of the cure

Turning to the final section of "The Direction of the Treatment", Eidelsztein emphasizes Lacan's claim that preserving the place of desire is fundamental to directing treatment. Demand has power, but desire is the motor. Desire makes itself visible through demand while remaining beyond demand, because it cannot be exhausted in anything explicitly asked for.

Eidelsztein gives "beyond" a determinative sense: what lies beyond demand is not an optional supplement but what determines demand. The subject reverberates between demands while trying to fix its being. Yet no new word can simply remove the mark imposed by previous speech. Each signifier represents the subject only for another signifier, so the hope for a final word that would absolve the subject of the effects of language only repeats the split.

The barred subject therefore designates more than ignorance. It marks the impossibility of a signifier that could cancel the effects of signification and yield an unmarked being. The question of being is opened precisely in the interval between demands.

Eidelsztein then contrasts identification with the all-powerful signifier of demand and identification with the object of demand for love. The first corresponds to suggestion: the subject conforms to an insignia attributed to the Other. The second can open the field of transference because the object requested in a demand for love necessarily fails to be fully deliverable. Moving from the omnipotent signifier to the vanishing object is thus a structural advance toward desire.

This is why frustration of demand has a technical function. It does not mean arbitrary deprivation. If the analyst simply gratifies demand, the analytic relation remains inside the circuit of demand. Frustration exposes the beyond of demand and allows the transferential object to become operative. Eidelsztein links this distinction to Lacan's later description of transference as the enactment of the sexual reality of the unconscious, not as suggestion.

### An axiomatic definition of fantasy

Eidelsztein then offers a compact formal definition: fantasy is a way of conceiving the barred subject, the object `a`, and the relation between them, represented by the lozenge in the fantasy formula. In an ordinary theory of knowledge, knowing subject and knowable object are constituted together in an epistemic relation. Psychoanalysis instead formalizes a relation in which both terms are lacking.

On the subject side there is fading, splitting, capture in the interval and the "ineffable" existence already described. On the object side there is disappearance or abolition: the object is not a positively present substance but is constituted through the play of presence and absence. Eidelsztein exploits Lacan's vocabulary of `fading`, fainting and syncope to emphasize that suppression occurs structurally on both sides.

Fantasy can therefore be defined clinically as the neurotic's position with respect to desire. It is not an imaginary story added to a pre-existing desire. It is the structure by which a subject answers demand and gives a particular signification to otherwise mythical "need".

### Fantasy interferes with signification

Eidelsztein distinguishes the signification supplied by the Other from the fantasy that interferes with that signification. At `s(A)` the subject receives its own message in inverted form from the Other. Fantasy does not itself own the signification; it returns from a wider circuit and modifies the point at which that signification is received.

[FIGURE: Schema 6, fantasy and `s(A)`]
Source location: printed p. 160 / PDF p. 161
Type: graph-of-desire pathway
Description: two arrows converge on `s(A)`: the lower circuit from the Other and a descending route from fantasy. The diagram isolates fantasy as the return point of a wider upper circuit that interferes with lower signification.
Labels visible in source: `s(A)`, `A`, fantasy position and surrounding graph pathways.
Directional structure: one route produces signification from the Other; the other descends from the upper question/fantasy circuit.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: shows formally why signification is "of the Other" while fantasy nonetheless modifies or obstructs it.
Fidelity note: visually checked.

The wider circuit is the circuit of the question, not the already described imaginary circuit. It carries demand to the limits of being, to the question "What am I?" The neurotic fantasy then returns into the lower graph and interferes at the very point where the Other's signification might otherwise close. The fantasy is thus both a support for desire and an obstacle within the circuit through which the subject seeks an answer from the Other.

### Fantasy sustains desire, not the choice of a correct object

Eidelsztein reads Lacan's criticism of Freud's handling of hysterical cases through this distinction. Freud often moved too quickly toward identifying the supposed object of love: Herr K for Dora, the brother-in-law in the Elisabeth von R. case, and so on. Lacan's objection is not primarily that Freud chose the wrong object. The deeper issue is that the object is structurally indifferent to the fundamental function of fantasy.

Fantasy is not a device that enables the subject to locate the "true" desired object. Its function is to sustain the subject in relation to desire, whether as desiring subject or as desired object. Dora's problem is therefore not settled by deciding who she really loved. The clinically relevant question is the fantasy through which she obstructed and sustained her own question of being.

Eidelsztein connects this to the analyst's silence. If the analyst does not answer demand, interpretation can preserve an allusive relation to the "disinhabited horizon of being" rather than fill it with a positive identity or object. Lacan's image of the raised finger of Leonardo's Saint John becomes spatially legible on the graph: it points upward toward the upper level, where drive and the signifier of a lack in the Other are located.

### The phallic signifier, the exit and the split subject

At the end of "Direction of the Treatment", Eidelsztein emphasizes Lacan's description of the phallus as an "unparalleled" or odd signifier. The phallus cannot be simply given or received in demand. The neurotic's problem of "having" it or "being" it is traversed only by accepting the impossibility on which that opposition rests.

The left side of the graph presents three different combinations of signifier and Other, culminating in the lack-in-the-Other notation. From desire `d`, an arrow reaches fantasy because there is no transparent, substantial "I desire" that could directly supply the subject's being. Fantasy sustains the subject in the being of desire.

[FIGURE: Schema 7, the two directions from fantasy]
Source location: printed p. 164 / PDF p. 165
Type: graph detail
Description: from desire `d` the path reaches fantasy. From the fantasy point, one direction descends into the lower graph while another goes upward toward the lack-in-the-Other position.
Directional structure: downward toward lower signification/ego/ideal circuits; upward toward the upper lack-signifier.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: formalizes two possible consequences of fantasy, either interference with lower signification or a route toward the "odd" signifier and an analytic exit.
Fidelity note: source page visually inspected.

The downward direction floods lower signification and returns the subject either to the metonymy of ego-signification or to petrification in an ideal. The upward direction points toward `S(Ⱥ)`, which Eidelsztein proposes can here be related to the phallic signifier. He calls this an "exit" from the trap produced when fantasy interferes with the signification of the Other. The route is associated with sublimation, the direction of the cure and the end of analysis.

### Desire as dissatisfied, impossible, prevented or will of jouissance

Eidelsztein closes through "Remark on Daniel Lagache's Report". Lacan's optical model belonged to an earlier moment in which it was necessary to clear away an overvalued imaginary. The later orientation returns attention to desire as what regulates the neurotic's signifying repetition and metonymy.

Desire is never encountered without a mode of support. In hysteria it is sustained as dissatisfied; in obsession it is sustained as impossible. Eidelsztein extends the same logic to phobia and perversion. The phobic object can function as a weapon against the disappearance of desire; the fetish can become an absolute condition of desire. Thus dissatisfied, prevented, impossible and will-of-jouissance positions are not mere descriptive adjectives. They name structural ways in which fantasy sustains desire through object `a`.

The conclusion is methodological as well as clinical: desire cannot be discussed in isolation. To speak rigorously of desire requires the fantasy that supports its position, and to work on fantasy requires following the oriented pathways through the graph.

## Chapter 9 - Desire and fantasme: A pathway (II)

<!--

### The neurotic attempt to turn desire into "I desire this"

Eidelsztein begins the second pathway chapter from a proposition he treats as fundamental: the neurotic expects desire to become a positive statement of the form "I desire this". Fantasy is the maneuver by which that conversion is attempted. The subject cannot simply pass beyond the question returned from the Other - `Che vuoi?`, reformulated as "What do you want of me?" - because the limitation is structural rather than a temporary failure of knowledge.

Two consequences follow. First, desire is not a private possession of the subject. Second, insofar as the subject is itself implicated as an object in the Other's desire, the Other does not know transparently what the subject is for it. The double opacity inscribes lack on both sides: lack in the desiring subject and lack in the desired object.

### Dissatisfied and impossible are positions toward desire, not kinds of desire

Eidelsztein revisits the common description of hysterical desire as dissatisfied and obsessional desire as impossible. He argues that these are not distinct species of desire. Desire itself is generated as the beyond of demand. What hysteria and obsession do is attempt to force that structurally unmasterable beyond back into the field of demand.

For the obsessional, "impossible desire" is a way of treating desire as though a sufficiently impossible demand could contain it. But no demand can cancel the effect it itself produces, namely the beyond called desire. In the formula Eidelsztein draws from "Direction of the Treatment", desire is the impossibility of a word that could undo the mark produced by speech.

The hysterical strategy has the same formal structure from the other side. Dissatisfaction belongs strictly to demand. To sustain desire as "unsatisfied desire" is therefore to translate the beyond of demand into the failure of a demand to be satisfied. The clinical labels describe the neurotic's position with respect to desire, not intrinsic modes of desire.

This is why fantasy must be added to the trio need-demand-desire. Fantasy marks the subject's response to the excess produced by demand. The Other supplies the signification of demand; fantasy intervenes as the return of the wider circuit in which demand reaches the limits of being and the subject appears to itself as lack.

### Subject as desire, not subject who possesses desire

Eidelsztein sharply distinguishes "the subject as desire" from "the subject insofar as it desires". The latter is already a neurotic fantasy of self-possession. In Lacan's formula, the subject localizes itself as lack in relation to both desiring and being desired. Desire is therefore not an attribute that a stable subject sometimes has. The desiring subject is the subject insofar as lack operates as agent and object.

The modern subject finds this double lack especially unbearable. Eidelsztein brings in Freud's contrast between ancient and modern erotic life: antiquity glorified the sexual activity or drive even with an inferior object, whereas modernity dignifies sexual activity through the merits of the chosen object. He connects Lacan's dating of the shift to courtly love and the elevation of woman as object.

The fantasy formula formalizes the modern maneuver. The fading subject is rescued from its eclipse by the proposition that it desires a particular object. Yet structurally the object cause of desire is indifferent to the empirical object. Fantasy reverses the relation by treating an object that functions as cause as though it were a condition: "I can desire if this object is there."

### Time, logic and space in the fantasy formula

Eidelsztein extracts three dimensions from the fantasy formula. The barred or fading subject is associated with a moment, hence time. The lozenge is associated with logic. The object `a`, insofar as fantasy presents it as a condition, is associated with extension and space.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, time-logic-space articulation of fantasy]
Source location: printed p. 172 / PDF p. 173
Type: tabular matheme analysis
Description: the fantasy formula is spread horizontally into three columns. Under the barred subject appear "Fading subject", "Moment" and "Time"; under the lozenge appears "Logics"; under `a` appear "Object as a condition", "Extension" and "Space".
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: decomposes fantasy into temporal, logical and spatial dimensions and prepares a structural comparison among neurosis, phobia and perversion.
Fidelity note: visually recoverable from source page.

Eidelsztein tentatively uses the distinction to organize clinical structures. Hysteria and obsession emphasize the subject on the temporal side, often too early or too late. Phobia and perversion accentuate the spatial staging of the object. The key addition, however, is the lozenge as logic. Drawing on Lacan's Seminar XI, Eidelsztein treats it as an algorithm rather than a pictorial relation.

Because it is an algorithm of letters, the fantasy formula does not constitute a metalanguage. Its elements do not carry one transcendent meaning valid for every case. Instead, the formula indicates an "absolute signification" produced in each case by fantasy. The empirical signification must therefore be established analytically rather than read directly out of the matheme.

### Fantasy as a machine for absolute signification

The ordinary signification of the Other is metonymic: one signification leads to another. Fantasy interferes with this movement by making one signification function as absolute. Eidelsztein therefore calls fantasy a machine that establishes conditions for the subject. It makes a contingent signification appear final, self-sufficient and object-linked.

This interference also explains fantasy's relation to castration. If every signification necessarily refers onward, no signification can terminate in a final object. Fantasy protects the subject from that dimension of castration by stopping the metonymic movement at an absolute condition.

### Homology between fantasy/desire and image/ego

Returning to the complete graph, Eidelsztein reads Lacan's claim that fantasy supports desire in a relation homologous to the way the other's image supports the ego. The homology is not immediately visible because the arrows are deliberately inverted.

[FIGURE: Schema 2, completed graph]
Source location: printed p. 174 / PDF p. 175
Type: complete graph of desire
Description: the full graph displays the lower imaginary and signification circuit, the intermediate desire/fantasy level and the upper drive/lack-in-the-Other level.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: provides the whole structure within which the fantasy-desire and image-ego homology must be read.
Fidelity note: source figure inspected through the PDF rendering.

### The graph is drawn through neurotic misrecognition

If the relation were drawn transparently, fantasy would support desire in the same direction as the other's image supports the ego. Instead, the graph reverses one pair. Eidelsztein reads this not as an error but as the formal inscription of `méconnaissance`. The graph itself is constructed in the order in which the neurotic encounters the problem: first the apparently obvious ego dialectic, then the less visible fantasy that determines it.

[FIGURE: Schema 3, homologous but inverted relations]
Source location: printed p. 175 / PDF p. 176
Type: paired relation schema
Description: fantasy and desire are placed on one line and ego `m` and image `i(a)` on another, with the apparent directions contrasted.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: shows that the graph intentionally masks determination in the same way neurotic experience masks it.
Fidelity note: source page checked.

Three things are structurally veiled: the ego is not a self-originating ego; desire is not the statement "I desire x" supplied by fantasy; and the ego/image dialectic is itself determined by the desire/fantasy dialectic. This hierarchy also explains Lacan's theoretical chronology. The mirror-stage problematic had to be elaborated before the deeper determination by fantasy could be formulated.

Eidelsztein uses Lacan's term `étoffe`, "stuff", to characterize fantasy as the material of the discursive `I`. The term suggests fabric, material for filling or clothing, and the quality or constitution of a thing. Fantasy supplies the material through which the subject can acquire a quality or condition in discourse. The discursive `I` is not identical with the symbolic subject; it is already a supported position made from fantasy's material.

### Lack in the Other and the question of what I am for it

A schema from Seminar X returns to the division between the Other's side and "my side". Lacan's dispute with Hegel becomes decisive: the Other is the unconscious, and the subject is involved in the Other precisely at the point of what the Other lacks and does not know. The route to what is lacking as the object of my desire therefore passes through the lack in the Other.

[FIGURE: Schema 4, subjective division]
Source location: printed p. 177 / PDF p. 178
Type: division schema
Description: two vertical domains, "Side of the Other" and "My side", organize `A`, subject-related terms and the remainder `a` across a division.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: introduces division as the formal operation through which subject and object `a` arise in relation to the Other.
Fidelity note: visually checked; exact typographic bars are treated separately in the notation register.

Eidelsztein stresses Lacan's preference for a formulation closer to "it did not know" over the simpler "it does not know". The point is not ignorance that could be repaired by more information. The temporally ambiguous formulation places knowledge itself under retroactive determination. What most concerns the subject's being of desire is what the Other lacked without knowing it.

No direct reference to a positive object can therefore support desire. The route must pass through the knot with an Other marked by lack, not merely the Other of demand.

### Division, quotient and remainder

Eidelsztein then reads Lacan's division schema mathematically. The subject is marked by the unary trait in the field of the Other and is inscribed as a quotient. Yet the division of the Other by the signifier never comes out without remainder. The remainder is object `a`, which guarantees that alterity is not exhausted by signifiers.

He maps the operation as follows: `A` is dividend, `S` divisor, the barred-subject term is quotient, and `a` is remainder. The question "How many times does S fit in A?" is a structural version of the subject's interrogation of the Other.

Division matters because, unlike addition or multiplication in the natural numbers, it can force the invention of another numerical domain. In Eidelsztein's analogy, the remainder is not a merely accidental bit of material that analysis has failed to enumerate. Even if an analysis could establish the signifiers of the Other exhaustively, the Other would not be annihilated because not everything in the Other is a signifier.

[FIGURE: Schema 5, division of the subject in the field of the Other]
Source location: printed p. 180 / PDF p. 181
Type: division schema
Description: the Other's side contains `A` and the remainder `a`; the subject-side column contains the corresponding signifying/division term. The layout is explicitly read as mathematical division.
Directional structure: the operation produces a quotient and an irreducible remainder.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: formalizes both fantasy's material dependence on the Other and the irreducible non-signifying remainder `a`.
Fidelity note: visual source inspected.

This resolves the earlier question of where fantasy belongs. Both the barred subject as marked in the Other and the remainder `a` are produced on the side of the Other. Fantasy is therefore entirely on that side. What remains on "my side" is the unconscious as interval, the lack in the Other that cannot be reduced to the material supplied by Oedipal history.

### From fantasy toward `S(Ⱥ)`

Eidelsztein interprets the direction of the cure as a pathway from the fantasy formula toward `S(Ⱥ)`. After the subject moves beyond ideals and identifies the historical material from which fantasy is woven, analysis does not end in a nihilistic "nothing". It reaches a more structural dimension: the status of the unconscious chain at the level of primal repression, where the subject is localized as pure lack.

The decisive object is no longer simply the historical content of the Other but what is lacking there. Eidelsztein is struck by the fact that the notation at this point still contains `S`, a signifier. Yet it is a signifier unlike the others, positioned outside the ordinary locus `A`. This exceptional signifier becomes the next problem of the book.

Before confronting it directly, however, Eidelsztein follows the route proposed in "Subversion of the Subject": he will pass through the upper-right position of the graph, the drive formula, and then move from drive toward the signifier of the lack in the Other. This mirrors the earlier path from `A` toward `s(A)` and establishes the program for the next chapters.

## Chapter 10 - The formula of the fantasme: Introduction to the drive

<!--
CHAPTER: 10
PDF_PAGES: 184-191
PRINTED_PAGES: 183-190

### Indestructible and unconscious desire

Eidelsztein begins by distinguishing structural attributes of desire from the neurotic strategies discussed in the previous chapter. "Impossible", "unsatisfied" and related predicates describe clinical positions toward desire; they are not intrinsic varieties of desire. If he had to assign general structural attributes, he would choose two: desire is indestructible and desire is unconscious.

Desire is indestructible because every demand to which a limit applies necessarily opens a beyond. Even the attempt "to desire not to desire" remains caught in that structure. Desire is unconscious because no demand can fully say or know what it produces beyond itself. Hence the Lacanian formula that desire is articulated but not articulable. What can be obtained at any moment is an interpretation of desire, not a final statement that captures it once and for all. Eidelsztein accordingly treats interpretation, itself a rhetorical operation, as structurally appropriate to desire and links analysis to the arts of well-saying.

### Fantasy, phantasy and the axiom

Eidelsztein distinguishes the structural `fantasme` from the predominantly imaginary phantasy in which it may appear. The formula of fantasy indicates a knotting of symbolic and real determinations that organizes the imaginary configuration. Phantasy is correlative to reality, whereas structural fantasy is what supports desire and frames the reality in which images and meanings appear.

The fundamental function of fantasy is axiomatic. An axiom does not derive its validity from a prior proof; it establishes the combinatory from which further consequences follow. Fantasy works similarly for the subject. It determines and justifies a set of symbolic and imaginary consequences while its own function is partly misrecognized.

Calling fantasy unconscious therefore does not mean merely that its sentence-content is absent from consciousness. In examples such as "A child is being beaten", the words may be known. What remains unconscious is the function that this phrasal structure performs for the subject. This leads directly to the drive, because Lacan's account of the drive is grammatical: the structure of a sentence, including transformations of voice and position, will prove more important than a supposedly natural instinctual content.

### Fantasy supports desire, the object does not

Drawing on Seminar XI, Eidelsztein emphasizes that fantasy, not object `a` by itself, supports desire. In fantasy the subject may be difficult to see, but it is always structurally present, split or doubled within a scenario. The apparent object also fails to show a simple "true face". The fantasy determines the subject as desiring through an ensemble of signifiers and roles.

The perverse fantasy is introduced because inversion makes the normal fantasy structure easier to see. In neurosis, the divided subject is sustained in relation to an object. In perversion, the subject places itself as object in relation to the division located in the partner.

[FIGURE: Schemas 1 and 2, direction of fantasy and perverse fantasy]
Source location: printed p. 186 / PDF p. 187
Type: matheme-direction diagrams
Description: the ordinary fantasy formula and the perverse use of the same formula are shown with opposed directional arrows. A separate proposed formula `a ◊ $` is distinguished from the perverse inversion.
Directional structure: perversion reverses the direction of the fantasy relation without simply exchanging the written positions of subject and object.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: distinguishes a perverse positioning of the subject-as-object from a possible analytic endpoint in which `a` functions as cause of the subject's division.
Fidelity note: formula direction checked against source text and figure.

The sadistic scene is Eidelsztein's example. The sadist's body, continuous with the whip, occupies the object-instrument position, while the victim's fainting stages subjective division. The point is not a moral characterization of sadism but the formal location of division in the partner and the subject's placement as object.

Object `a` is therefore never simply the aim of desire. It can be presubjective, a basis for identification or a basis for identification disavowed by the subject. What ordinary speech calls the "object of desire" is, in Lacan's account, either a lure or a fantasy that supports desire.

### Fantasy as scene, frame and border

Eidelsztein develops the notion of scene from Freud's primordial scene to the transferential scene of analysis. Roles can be read even when no explicit statement names them. The structural scene is supplied by fantasy, not by images alone. Its true basis is the script or plot, which Eidelsztein links to Freud's "tissue" and Lacan's `étoffe`.

He then analyzes the lozenge in the fantasy formula. Rather than a filled surface, it should first be understood as a border composed from logical operators.

[FIGURE: Schemas 3 and 4, logical border of the lozenge]
Source location: printed p. 188 / PDF p. 189
Type: logical decomposition and topological border diagram
Description: the lozenge is decomposed into four directional/logical elements associated with minor/major and conjunction/disjunction; a second schema contrasts a filled surface with a border enclosing a void.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: establishes the lozenge as a punctuating border and prepares the concepts of frame, erogenous rim and cut.
Fidelity note: source figure visually inspected in extraction/render workflow.

For fantasy, this border is the frame of the fantasy. The frame makes reality visible by limiting it, while remaining itself relatively invisible. Eidelsztein uses the scopic field to make the point. Reality is organized by what is subtracted from view, and the gaze as object `a` is especially hidden precisely because it structures the visual field.

Magritte's *The Human Condition* provides the exemplary scene: painting, window and represented landscape overlap so that the frame is thematized through its disappearance. The border of the eyelids supplies an even more elementary example. The field of sight is organized by a limit that normally does not appear as an object within the field it makes possible. A pathological irruption such as feeling a gaze at one's back can then be read as the emergence into reality of what should have functioned through subtraction.

### Veil, screen and traversing fantasy

Fantasy functions both as veil and as screen. As veil, it conceals the subtraction of object `a`; as screen, it supplies a surface on which images can be projected. Eidelsztein refuses to resolve this apparent contradiction by choosing one function. Their continuity is topological: what is moved away through concealment is approached by passing through the veil, because the lack hidden by the scene can emerge precisely where the scene is traversed.

He uses the theatrical notion of a practicable set-piece, a painted door or window that is also literally passable. It is false as scenery and true as an opening. This provides his model for "traversing the fantasy". The aim is not to expose fantasy as simply false. It is to encounter the way truth itself has the structure of fiction for the subject and to pass through the arrangement by which fantasy frames and veils lack.

### From suggestion to transference

Before treating drive, Eidelsztein reconstructs Lacan's changing theory of transference. An early schema opposed imaginary suggestion, tied to the little other, to symbolic transference, tied to the big Other. Seminar XI makes that mapping insufficient. Suggestion can now be understood as the effect produced when an ordinary other is elevated to the position of the Other. This recognition is necessary for analysis but is not identical with transference.

Transference becomes the enactment of the sexual reality of the unconscious. On the graph, it is not simply located at `A`. To remain at `A` would preserve the power of the supposed Other. The analyst must sustain the interval between the lower and upper signifying chains.

[FIGURE: Schema 5, completed graph used to locate transference]
Source location: printed p. 193 / PDF p. 194
Type: completed graph of desire
Description: the full two-level graph is reproduced so that the interval between the lower and upper chains can be distinguished from the point `A` itself.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: locates transference in the between-two of the chains rather than equating it with the analyst's occupation of the Other position.
Fidelity note: complete graph checked against source.

Not satisfying demand is therefore not a simple "no". Analytic technique works by making yes and no operate together: accepting the demand for analysis while refusing to answer it in the form expected. Eidelsztein identifies this interval with the desire of the analyst. The analysand's elevation of the analyst to a knowing Other is the subject-supposed-to-know maneuver; the analyst's task is not to settle into that place.

If the analyst closes the interval by meeting demand as knowing Other, acting out can appear as the response of the desiring subject. Eidelsztein treats such acting out as connected to a fall of analytic function, not because the analyst simply ceased being an Other but because the analyst failed to sustain the interval beyond demand.

### Klein group and the two dimensions of interval

To formalize the superior chain, Eidelsztein introduces the mathematical notion of group and especially the Klein four-group. A group is a set whose elements are linked by operations. The Klein group has four elements and three non-trivial transformations, each of which returns to the starting point when applied twice; composing two produces the third.

[FIGURE: Schemas 6 and 7, Klein-group construction]

Description: a first schema arranges four elements using circles/squares and light/dark distinctions. A second connects four corner-elements with differently patterned edges corresponding to the three group operations.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: supplies a formal model in which horizontal and vertical relations can be transformed without collapsing into identity.
Fidelity note: diagram structure read from source; decorative line styles are not semantically renamed beyond the author's explanation.

Eidelsztein maps this structure onto the graph of desire. Lower and upper functions must be homologous but transformed. One cut can separate `S1` from `S2`; another separates the lower chain from the upper chain. Together they establish two dimensions of interval that define the unconscious.

[FIGURE: Schema 8, complete graph with two cuts]
Source location: printed p. 197 / PDF p. 198

Role in Eidelsztein's argument: formalizes the unconscious through a pair of articulated intervals rather than a hidden content located behind consciousness.
Fidelity note: source figure visually checked.

### Closed structure, finite desire and the upper transformation

Eidelsztein asks whether the two practicable cuts can be iterated without limit. If they could, analysis would have no possible closure. He therefore returns to the interior-eight topology as the structure that puts the two intervals in continuity within a closed surface. One pair is `S1-S2`; the other is lower chain-upper chain. A complete theory must articulate not only each pair but the relation between their intervals.

This closure also underwrites his claim that desire is finite and limited, despite the neurotic fantasy of metonymic infinity. He contrasts this with psychosis, where the extraction of object `a` and the desire/fantasy structure are not established in the same way.

The Klein-group logic now makes a specific prediction: the lower-right function `A`, the treasure of signifiers, should have a transformed homolog on the upper right. Lacan names that transformed function the drive.

### Drive as a localization of the subject in the body

The drive formula initially seems paradoxical because Lacan writes demand rather than "body". Eidelsztein resolves the problem by asking how the primordially repressed subject can be localized in the upper chain. It cannot appear straightforwardly as the grammatical subject of a statement or as a transparent enunciator. Lacan's answer is that the drive localizes the subject in an organic zone at precisely the point where the body "speaks" without the subject being the one who knowingly speaks.

Pain or disturbance in a drive-related organ makes this structure evident. The subject asks, "What does this mean?" The organ has become a message-bearing site, yet the subject does not experience itself as the author of that message. Drive thus provides another localization of the subject of the unconscious, different from the fantasy localization of the subject as desire.

The barred subject in the drive formula is therefore appropriate: the subject is represented where the body speaks, but cannot be directly present as master of that speech.

### Synchrony, diachrony and the remainder of demand

Eidelsztein uses Lacan's description of the drive as a transformed "treasure of the signifiers" to distinguish the two levels. `A` on the lower chain has a fundamentally synchronic character: for the arriving subject, language is already there. The upper formula transforms that treasure by linking it to diachrony.

When the subject disappears in demand, demand itself also disappears as a determinate message. What remains is the cut. The drive is distinguished from the organic function it inhabits by this cut and by its grammatical artifice.

The erogenous zone is therefore not the whole biological organ. It is a border: lips, teeth, throat or another rim. What the body offers as real for unconscious localization is precisely what has the structure of a cut. Eidelsztein applies the distinction to psychosomatic lesions: a lesion can introduce a cut where the ordinary corporal topology did not offer one, suggesting a failure of interval or holophrastic functioning rather than an ordinary drive rim.

### Grammar as the treasure of signifiers on the upper chain

If the lower `A` is commonly imagined as a vocabulary of words and meanings, the transformed treasure on the upper chain is grammar. Grammar is a knowledge speakers constantly apply without necessarily knowing that they know it. It is shared by speakers and structures possible utterances independently of the particular message.

This explains Lacan's insistence on the grammar of the drive. The oral drive is not defined simply by a substance such as milk. Suction can be transformed grammatically into being sucked or sucking oneself. Active, passive and reflexive voices articulate the drive's reversals of source and object.

The drive therefore joins three structures: the subject's fading, demand as speech, and a bodily cut organized through grammar and diachrony.

[FIGURE: Schema 9, graph as Klein group]
Source location: printed p. 203 / PDF p. 204
Type: four-corner Klein-group rendering of graph functions
Description: four graph positions occupy the corners of a square-like structure, with differentiated connecting lines corresponding to the group operations. The lower pair is related to signification/Other and the upper pair to lack/drive.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: summarizes the chapter's claim that upper graph functions are transformations, not repetitions, of the lower functions.
Fidelity note: structure and labels checked against source extraction and page rendering; exact barred notation is audited separately.

The chapter therefore arrives at the drive not by importing an instinct theory but by following the internal transformation rules of the graph. The next task is to develop the upper-right formula in its own right before passing from it to the upper-left signifier of the lack in the Other.

## Chapter 11 - The drive (I)

### Seminar XI, science and the refounding of the drive

Eidelsztein situates Seminar XI in Lacan's institutional rupture with the International Psychoanalytical Association. Lacan's comparison of his exclusion with Spinoza's excommunication leads him to diagnose the psychoanalytic institution as church-like. Eidelsztein reads the Seminar's "four fundamental concepts" as Lacan's attempt to prevent psychoanalysis from resting on orthodoxy by refounding its concepts in an articulation with science.

The drive is therefore approached not as inherited doctrine but as a concept to be reconstructed. Eidelsztein organizes the task around Lacan's notions of montage and deconstruction: the formula of the drive, the four elements into which Freud decomposes it, and the four partial drives Lacan privileges. He postpones the separate question of the drive's vicissitudes.

### Drive is not an organic hinge

The formula `($ ◊ D)` is read against the widespread idea that drive mediates between biology and psyche. Lacan's wager, as Eidelsztein presents it, is stronger: there is nothing natural about drive. Sexuality enters psychic life through the montage of the partial drives, and this montage must conform to the gap-like structure of the unconscious.

The lozenge can therefore be read as an interval operator. The drive is articulated to the gaps produced between signifiers rather than to a continuous energetic push from the organism. Sexuality reaches the speaking being only through what passes into the networks of the signifier. Since mathematical network and graph are structurally related, Eidelsztein treats each subject's signifying system as the net in which sexuality is represented.

What does not enter the net is lost. This loss makes total sexuality impossible to represent. Only partial drives remain. The partiality is not a developmental immaturity awaiting genital completion; it follows from the signifier's inability to inscribe an "all" of sexuality. The post-Freudian ideal of completed genitality is therefore itself an effect of the lack of total representation.

Love enters at the same point. Freud already separates love from a complete representation of sexual impulse. Eidelsztein reads demand `D` in the drive formula as demand for love: where the partial drives cannot supply totality, love appears as an attempt to recover it. The drive represents sexuality rather than presenting a biological sexuality directly, and its montage is imposed by the signifying net.

### Sexuality, death and the headless subject

Heraclitus's bow gives Eidelsztein a figure for Lacan's claim that the drive traces a curve of sexuality. The curve ends in death because sexual reproduction at the level of the species structurally links generation to the death of preceding generations. Eidelsztein distinguishes this real death from symbolic death while recalling Freud's recurrent conjunction of sexuality and death.

The barred-subject term of the drive formula is then treated through Lacan's image of a "headless subject". The relation between the subject at the graph's point of departure and the barred subject in the drive formula is one of topological community, not simple identity. The subject of drive is a subjectification without an already placed subject.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, completed graph and topological community of barred-subject positions]
Source location: printed p. 211 / PDF p. 212
Type: completed graph of desire
Description: the completed graph is used to compare the barred-subject point from which the graph departs with the barred-subject term in the drive formula on the upper right.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: establishes a topological relation between distinct subject positions without collapsing them into one occurrence of the same symbol.
Fidelity note: full graph checked against source layout.

Lacan's losange marks the gaps created by the distribution of signifying investments. Eidelsztein places alongside them the gaps of the "apparatus of the body". This apparatus is not the biological organism but an artificial-like system of parts and holes. Drive becomes possible because the holes in the bodily apparatus and the intervals in the signifying network have a common topological structure.

The drive thus represents a gap within a gap. The lozenge can simultaneously formalize the bodily rim of the erogenous zone and the interval between signifiers.

### Neurosis, perversion and subject-position in the drive

Because the drive is "headless", the subject is structurally not yet placed in it. Eidelsztein stresses that this "not yet" is logical, not developmental. Perversion is defined by what happens when a subject takes a position in this structure: it places itself as object `a`, instrument of the Other's jouissance.

### Reciprocal transformations of fantasy and drive

Eidelsztein formalizes Freud's neurosis/perversion opposition by tracking how Lacan's formulae transform. In perversion, the drive structure becomes the fantasy insofar as the subject places itself as object. In neurosis, fantasy is reduced toward the drive because the neurotic identifies the lack in the Other with demand and substitutes demand `D` for object `a`: the subject demands to be demanded.

[FIGURE: Schemas 3 and 4, perverse fantasy and neurosis/perversion transformations]
Source location: printed pp. 214-215 / PDF pp. 215-216
Type: directional matheme diagrams
Description: one schema shows the ordinary fantasy formula with reversed direction for perversion; another places neurosis and perversion in parallel columns and shows transformations between fantasy and drive formulae.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: gives a formal, closed set of transformations rather than multiplying ad hoc clinical formulae.
Fidelity note: formulas checked against source text; exact bar glyphs audited separately.

Eidelsztein emphasizes that Lacan's mathemes are not freely inventable. Their number and transformation rules form a closed structure unless a reason is given to alter it. Clinical interpretation should therefore respect the formal constraints rather than invent new formulas for every phenomenon.

### Subject-with-holes, lost object and the lamella

Lacan's "headless subjectification" has two topological aspects. On one side is a subject without a head, a structural outline rather than a person-like agent. On the other is the `sujet troué`, the subject-with-holes produced through the signifier. Eidelsztein draws the consequence that the subject is related both to the surface bearing the holes and to what is localized in the holes.

Object `a` is present in the drive as lost object. The lamella myth gives this loss a bodily metaphor: the lost part is a part of the subject's own body rather than a piece removed from the Other. Lacan's placenta example matters because the placenta is fetal tissue. The lost object is localized in the gaps of the subject's bodily apparatus.

This makes drive a montage rather than a biological unity. Freud's pressure, aim, object and source must be deconstructed because the four terms do not naturally form one coherent instinct. Even the pressure is unlike biological rhythm: it is characterized as constant.

Eidelsztein links this to the "Freudian field" as a two-dimensional topological field, contrasting it with the complete three-dimensional organism. The nervous system matters structurally as a network of connections and intervals; its precise metric shape is secondary. Freud's description of the ego as a psychical representation of the bodily surface is re-read as a signifying representation of a surface with holes.

### Against psychic energy: satisfaction and dissatisfaction on one surface

Eidelsztein briefly suspends a full account of jouissance because, in his view, the concept cannot be understood while psychoanalysis continues to think in terms of psychic energy. The properties assigned to physical energy do not transfer to Lacanian jouissance.

He instead takes up the drive's aim. Freud identifies aim with satisfaction, but sublimation already shows that satisfaction can occur without the supposedly natural aim being reached. Lacan uses this contradiction to dissolve the ordinary opposition between satisfaction and dissatisfaction. Symptom formation and preliminary pleasure show that what satisfies can simultaneously dissatisfy.

Eidelsztein models the continuity topologically through the Möbius strip. There are not two separately existing sides called satisfaction and dissatisfaction; there are positions along one continuous surface that can be experienced as opposite. The drive therefore inscribes the impossibility of obtaining a satisfaction that could remain simply satisfactory.

The ethical consequence is important. The limit of drive does not arise from an internal measure of satisfaction. It is supplied by ethics. Analysis intervenes not against the ordinary discontent of civilization as such but when a subject encounters an excess of suffering, Lacan's `trop de mal`.

### Aim as circuit and object `a` as the hole circumvented

The drive's aim is the return into circuit. Eidelsztein follows Lacan's play on `tour` as turn and trick. The drive goes around an object and returns; its satisfaction is in the circuit rather than in obtaining a biologically adequate object.

Object `a` is not the original food or the positive object on which the oral drive closes. No food can satisfy the oral drive as such because the circuit is organized around an eternally lacking object. Eidelsztein therefore distinguishes two apparent object-functions: an empirical object that can close the circuit like a plug, and object `a` as the lack or hole around which the circuit actually turns. The first is the "trick" that conceals the second.

[FIGURE: Schemas 5 and 6, object closing the hole vs object `a` as hole]

Fidelity note: source diagrams visually inspected.

Eidelsztein then topologically deforms Lacan's drawing to eliminate the misleading suggestion of a third dimension in which the drive would travel "outward" to fetch an object. By inclining and continuously transforming the figure, he keeps erogenous zone, drive path and hole in one two-dimensional topology.

The source or erogenous zone is correspondingly a bodily border or hole, not the full organ. Which bodily border acquires drive-function depends on the history of demand, especially the demand of the Other. The oral zone may therefore be lips, teeth or throat according to the subject's particular articulation.

The chapter closes by returning to the graph itself. Eidelsztein's earlier proposal to close the graph as an interior eight is now justified through the drive: the graph's pathway contains an internal hole, and the circuit of the drive demonstrates why border, interval and return must be thought topologically.
