### Perversion revisited: the fantasy that the perverse subject enjoys without limit

Eidelsztein begins by returning to perversion in order to challenge what he calls a neurotic fantasy: that the perverse subject is uniquely free to enjoy. Lacan's structural account implies the opposite. In perversion, the drive is especially constrained by fantasy because the subject abandons the headless, "not yet placed" position of the drive and takes a definite place within it.

The temporal word "yet" must not be read developmentally. There is no later maturational stage in which the subject naturally comes to occupy the drive. In ordinary drive structure the subject remains logically unplaced. Eidelsztein links this to Lacan's later reference to the "silence of the drive": the drive is not mute; rather, the more "it" speaks, the less the subject speaks as conscious author.

### The perverse subject as object-cause in the scene

In perversion the subject takes the position of object `a`. This is why the drive formula and fantasy formula converge. The direction of fantasy is inverted: the subject presents itself as the object that causes the partner's division.

[FIGURE: Schemas 1 and 2, drive/fantasy coincidence and inverted direction]
Source location: printed pp. 226-227 / PDF pp. 226-227
Type: formula transformation diagrams
Description: the drive and fantasy formulae are aligned to show their coincidence when the subject takes the object position; the following schema marks a reversal of direction in the fantasy relation.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: formalizes perversion as a positioning of the subject at `a`, not as greater instinctual freedom or greater quantity of jouissance.
Fidelity note: formulas checked against source text and page image structure.

Eidelsztein works through four Freudian perversions while deliberately setting fetishism aside as anomalous to this series. The exhibitionist offers a part of the body to the other's gaze. The masochist can offer the whole self as contractual object. The sadist makes a bodily part, such as the arm continuous with a torture instrument, function as object of jouissance while the victim stages the divided subject. The voyeur is more complicated because simply looking through a keyhole would leave the voyeur in an ordinary desiring-subject position.

The specifically perverse voyeuristic scene requires a public setting and the possible gaze of a third party. The voyeur must in turn be available to be seen looking. The divided subject is therefore not simply the voyeur or the person observed; the scene is organized so that the voyeur becomes an object offered to another gaze. In all four cases, the perverse fiction is that the subject-as-object causes the other's division and thereby veils the structural lack in the Other.

### The subject and the lost part in the drive

Leaving perversion, Eidelsztein returns to neurosis and the double localization of the subject in drive. The subject can be thought as the bodily apparatus with holes and, at another level, as what is localized in those holes. This apparent overlap with object `a` is clarified through the lamella: the object is a lost part of the subject's own body. The subject's object is thus, structurally, a lost part of the subject.

[FIGURE: Schema 3, erogenous zone and field of the Other]

Type: drive topology schema
Description: the erogenous zone is represented as the border of a hole; the subject is written at the hole, with the unconscious or field of the Other represented beyond/alongside the bodily apparatus.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: identifies the lost object with a lost part of the subject rather than with a positive object possessed by the Other.
Fidelity note: source figure visually recoverable; topology described rather than redrawn.

Eidelsztein reinforces the point with Freud's distinction between "being" and "having" the object. The child's primitive formula is closer to "I am the breast"; "I have it" appears after loss and simultaneously implies "I am not it". A substitute object occupying the lost place can therefore conceal the loss by its very presence.

### Turn, trick and the creel

Lacan's play on `tour` allows Eidelsztein to distinguish the object around which the drive turns from the empirical object on which it seems to close. The drive is both a turn around a nothing and a trick that prevents the subject from seeing that its circuit is organized around an eternally lacking object.

The erogenous zone has the structure of a border, not a surface. It should not be confused with an extended biological tract such as the digestive system. Eidelsztein then uses Lacan's creel, a fishing basket with an inward funnel, to represent the logic of a closed surface that can trap an object while organizing a repeatable circuit around an opening.

### Partial drive and interior eight

Eidelsztein contrasts Lacan's schema of the partial drive with the interior eight. The comparison requires distinguishing `aim` from `goal`. The drive can hit its target without ever leaving the circuit that returns it to its point of departure. Its "goal" is not biological completion but the return itself.

[FIGURE: Schema 5, partial drive and interior eight]
Source location: printed p. 231 / PDF p. 231
Type: comparative topological diagrams
Description: Lacan's partial-drive circuit is placed beside an interior-eight form. Both represent departure and return without a simple container/contained relation.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: shows that the drive's inversion and return can be formalized as a continuous topology rather than a linear acquisition of an object.
Fidelity note: source comparison visually inspected.

Every drive movement brings its reversal. Eidelsztein links this to demand: what is sent to the Other returns in inverted form. Partiality therefore concerns not only failure to reach a biological totality but the to-and-fro structure of the circuit itself.

The interior eight also allows Eidelsztein to reject three-dimensional container models, including Freud's "ovum" schema. Inside and outside are not simply separated volumes. In the interior eight, exterior can be included in interior through the continuity of the surface. The drive can thus circle a border without generating an object capable of finally plugging the hole.

The interior eight is the border of a Möbius strip and is also related to the structure of the torus. Its theoretical importance is repetition: whenever a circuit attempts to repeat itself, signifying structure makes identical repetition impossible. Redoubling produces difference and antinomy, while simultaneously producing the impulse to try again. Eidelsztein treats this failed repetition as one of the central structures of the discontent of civilization.

### The drive does not enter the Other by itself

Eidelsztein warns that the usual drawing can create the illusion that the drive traverses the field of the Other. Pure drive satisfaction does not require the Other. What knots drive to the Other is desire and love. This distinction prevents the Other from being smuggled into every bodily circuit merely because the drive has signifying structure.

### Why oral precedes anal without natural development

The order of the partial drives cannot be explained by a natural metamorphosis. Lacan explicitly denies a relation of biological production in which one partial drive develops into the next. Yet the oral-anal order is not arbitrary. Eidelsztein explains it through demand.

Orality comes first logically because the infant's cry is interpreted by an Other as an appeal. This transformation of cry into call is the beginning of the human dialectic of demand. Once the Other receives a demand, the structural inversion follows: the subject receives its own demand from the Other in inverted form. Anality, especially sphincter control, stages this inversion as the Other now demanding something from the subject.

The excrement-money-gift series is therefore intelligible as a series of objects offered in response to the Other's demand. The order is signifying and relational, not biologically programmed.

The scopic and invocatory drives differ. Gaze and voice are more directly tied to the object of desire than to the object of demand and therefore do not simply extend the oral-anal gift series. The gaze appears as what is missing from the visible field; the voice is what disappears or is forgotten in the field of speech.

The chapter thus consolidates the drive as a non-natural montage of border, demand, grammar, loss and circuit. Its order is generated by the dialectic of the Other, while its satisfaction remains organized around a hole that no positive object can permanently close.

### Sources used

- Alfredo Eidelsztein, *The Graph of Desire: Using the Work of Jacques Lacan*, Chapter 12, printed pp. 225-234, project PDF pp. 225-234.

### `S(Ⱥ)` as the transformed closure of signification

Eidelsztein introduces `S(Ⱥ)` as one of the book's most difficult problems and organizes the chapter around being, jouissance and desire. He begins from Lacan's claim that every signifying chain tends to loop its signification. On the lower chain, the familiar pair is the treasure of signifiers `A` and the signified of the Other `s(A)`. The completed graph reproduces this logic on the upper level, but through transformed functions.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, lower and upper code/message relations]
Source location: printed p. 236 / PDF p. 236
Type: four-term transformation schema
Description: Jakobson's message/code pair `(M)-(C)` and a transformed upper pair `(M)'-(C)'` are aligned with `s(A)-A` and their upper-level homologues. Vertical links indicate transformation between lower and upper functions.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: introduces the proposition that `S(Ⱥ)` performs, at the unconscious/enunciation level, a function homologous to the closure of signification performed by `s(A)` below.
Fidelity note: source diagram visually checked; barred-A notation visually verified as `S(Ⱥ)`.

The apparent paradox is deliberate. `S(Ⱥ)` is a signifier, yet it is placed on the side homologous to signification. Eidelsztein therefore reads the upper level through the opposition statement/enunciation, now reformulated as content of what is said versus act of saying. The relevant effect is produced not by a new message-content but by unconscious enunciation as act.

The Other is required by `Che vuoi?` to answer for the value of its treasure. Eidelsztein pauses over the word "treasure": it designates both valuables and the place that contains them, but it also implies incompleteness. The upper question asks what the Other is worth as the locus of signifiers and receives its answer at the level of unconscious enunciation.

### No Other of the Other and no final guarantee

The lack written in `S(Ⱥ)` is the lack inherent in the Other's function as treasure of signifiers. Eidelsztein links this directly to Lacan's formula "there is no Other of the Other". There is no further locus that could guarantee the Other, just as there is no metalanguage capable of standing outside language and guaranteeing its consistency without itself entering the same problem.

At the lower level the subject already depends on the Other for punctuation and signification: the signification of one's own message is received from the Other. The stronger upper-level thesis is that this guarantor is itself without guarantee. The supposed final authority therefore cannot supply a last true word.

Eidelsztein names the resulting problem "No-Faith". Language allows the subject to lie even by telling the truth, as the Krakow/Lemberg joke illustrates. Hence the analyst, who occupies the place from which the Other is made to speak in the analytic situation, cannot legitimately claim to pronounce an ultimate doctrine. Psychoanalysis is not the transmission of a religious final truth.

The apparently radical answer "God is dead" is also insufficient. It can become another religious or philosophical last word, another supposed truth guaranteed by a dead Father. The analytic route must go further.

[FIGURE: Schema 2, pathway from `A` through drive to `S(Ⱥ)`]
Source location: printed p. 238 / PDF p. 238
Type: upper/lower graph relation
Description: `A` on the lower right is linked upward toward the drive formula, while the upper-left `S(Ⱥ)` is linked with the left side of the graph; the pathway implies that access to the lack in the Other passes through the drive and therefore the body.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: prevents `S(Ⱥ)` from being reduced to an abstract logical lack detached from drive, body and jouissance.
Fidelity note: schematic relation checked against source page.

### Dead Father, empty tomb and going beyond the Father

Eidelsztein reads Lacan's contrast among Abraham, Moses and Christ as a distinction between the corpse as signifier and the empty tomb as hole. The dead Father can indeed function as signifier, and the Name-of-the-Father belongs to that register. But identifying the paternal signifier does not resolve the structural lack indicated by the empty grave.

Moses and Christ are treated as legislators whose deaths can support a signifying myth. Abraham points instead toward the pact, circumcision, proper name and the alteration of names. Eidelsztein cautiously marks this as his hypothesis about Lacan's difficult allusion: the relevant issue is not merely paternal legislation but operations of naming and the phallic signifier that are structurally "beyond the Father".

Going beyond the Father therefore does not mean replacing the Father with the analyst as embodiment of the dead Father or as mouthpiece of a final truth. It means moving from paternal guarantee toward the structural problem of the signifier and its lack. Psychoanalysis differentiates itself from religion precisely at this point.

### Beginning again from `S(Ⱥ)`

Eidelsztein emphasizes Lacan's surprising phrase "I will begin" near the end of "Subversion of the Subject". The absence of final truth does not terminate analytic work in nothingness. It requires beginning from the hole.

`S(Ⱥ)` is first of all a signifier. Lacan's definition remains that a signifier represents the subject for another signifier. The exceptional signifier is the one because of which the other signifiers can represent the subject; in its absence, the others would represent nothing, since representation is always for something else. The next problem is therefore to understand how a signifier can perform this exceptional function without becoming a new Other of the Other.

<!--

### Treasure, battery and the signifier outside the locus of signifiers

Eidelsztein distinguishes Lacan's metaphors of treasure and battery. A treasure is intrinsically incomplete: its value depends on scarcity and on what is not included. A battery or set, by contrast, can be complete with whatever number of elements defines it. When Lacan calls `A` the battery of signifiers, the logical problem becomes acute: if all signifiers are in `A`, how can there also be the signifier `S(Ⱥ)` outside `A`?

[FIGURE: Schema 3, four graph positions as Klein-group transformations]
Source location: printed p. 242 / PDF p. 242
Type: four-corner functional schema
Description: upper left `S(Ⱥ)` is labeled "Signifier of a lack in (A)"; upper right is the drive formula and "Treasure of the unconscious signifier"; lower left is `s(A)`, "Signified of the Other"; lower right is `A`, "Battery of the signifier (all of the signifiers)". Horizontal arrows and vertical arrows connect the four positions.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: isolates the anomaly that a signifier is positioned outside the locus containing all signifiers and on the side homologous to signification.
Fidelity note: visually checked at PDF p. 242; barred `A` verified in the printed figure.

The problem is not solved by calling the exceptional term an unknown, hole or absence. Lacan insists on calling it a signifier. Eidelsztein contrasts it with the Name-of-the-Father. Earlier Lacanian formulations risked making the Name-of-the-Father the signifier that legislates all others, hence an Other of the Other. The later logic requires the paternal signifier to be a signifier among signifiers. Only `S(Ⱥ)` is structurally different, and it is different precisely because it cannot be counted as a member of the battery it makes possible.

### The extra turn that cannot be counted with the others

Eidelsztein relates this exceptional signifier to Lacan's necklace/ring topology and to the torus of repeated demand. The signifiers are like linked rings; demand makes repeated turns around a void. Yet the total circulation produces an additional turn that cannot be counted in the same series as the individual turns.

[FIGURE: Schema 4, repeated turns on a torus]
Source location: printed p. 243 / PDF p. 243
Type: toroidal/repetition schema
Description: repeated demand-turns coil around a central void, with the overall traversal producing a structurally different extra turn.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: models the exceptional signifier as a turn generated by the series but not countable as one more member of the same series.
Fidelity note: figure visually checked.

The Earth's rotations and revolution supply an intuitive analogy. Daily rotations can be counted in a series, while the annual revolution is another turn of a different order. It is both an extra turn and, relative to the daily count, a turn that cannot simply be added as another day. `S(Ⱥ)` is similarly a signifying trace generated by the system but not countable in its ordinary inventory.

### Proper name and the inherence of minus one

Lacan symbolizes the operation by the inherence of `-1` in the set of signifiers. The exceptional signifier is inexpressible as a positive member, but its operation is not inexpressible. Eidelsztein locates that operation whenever a proper name is uttered. A proper name seems to represent the subject in a singular way, and its enunciation foregrounds the act of naming rather than merely a lexical meaning.

The paradox is that saying "one signifier is lacking" already fills the place with a signifier and thus denies the lack it states. The Name-of-the-Father cannot solve this because it would plug the hole with a particular paternal signifier. Eidelsztein again relates the problem to the Abrahamic pact, in which both God's name and the transformed human names involve the problem of an unpronounceable or structurally singular name.

The Saussurean algorithm helps clarify the issue. Ordinarily a signifier stands over a bar resisting signification, with a signified below. For `S(Ⱥ)`, nothing positive can simply be written in the place of the exceptional term without replacing the lack. Proper names offer a limiting case in which statement and signification approach equivalence and the operation of the signifier becomes visible.

### Mathematical analogues: π, e and `i`

Eidelsztein turns to Kasner and Newman's *Mathematics and the Imagination* to show how mathematics works productively with symbols that common sense cannot reduce to ordinary numbers. `π` and `e` cannot be finitely expressed by a terminating or repeating decimal; they function as precise procedures or limits rather than ordinary completed quantities.

The imaginary unit `i = √-1` sharpens the analogy. No real number squared yields `-1`, yet mathematics introduces a symbol governed by exact operational rules. Its apparent impossibility does not make it arbitrary; it makes possible an enlarged system in which directions, forces and other structures can be represented.

[FIGURE: Schemas 5 and 6, geometric mean and complex plane]
Source location: printed pp. 246-247 / PDF pp. 246-247
Type: mathematical diagrams
Description: a right-triangle construction illustrates the geometric mean; the following Cartesian/Gaussian plane places positive and negative axes so that a geometric-mean construction yields `√-1 = i`.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: gives a mathematical model for a precise symbol that is not an ordinary member of the prior numerical domain, paralleling the exceptional formal status of `S(Ⱥ)`.
Fidelity note: equations and axes visually checked against source pages.

Eidelsztein does not claim that `S(Ⱥ)` literally is an imaginary number. The analogy concerns formal existence: a symbol can be rigorously necessary and operationally productive while violating the common-sense ontology of the domain from which the problem arose.

### What the cogito cannot exhaust

The mathematical discussion returns to the subject. `S(Ⱥ)` marks what the subject lacks in order to think itself as exhausted by the cogito. The problem is not an empirically unknown fact that could later be learned. It is what is unthinkable from within the position that seeks to secure being through "I think".

Eidelsztein follows Lacan into the difficulty of speaking about the being of the speaking subject. The pronoun `I` is a shifter: every attempt to state what the subject is necessarily stages an enunciation in which the speaker appears again. The problem cannot be solved from outside language because talking about the speaking subject repeats the structure under investigation.

Love can prove the existence of the Other for a subject, but this does not prove the subject's own being. The question is therefore not simply "Who am I?" as a request for recognition but "What am I?" at the point where no final signifier answers.

### Voice, Non-Being and the place of jouissance

Lacan's answer places the subject where a voice is heard clamoring that the universe is a defect in the purity of Non-Being. Eidelsztein emphasizes that the relevant object is the voice as object, not the semantic content of the utterance. The signifier has a mortifying or "nothingifying" effect, but that effect is never total. Something remains as an impurity in Non-Being: the object attached to enunciation, exemplified by voice.

This remaining place is called jouissance. Eidelsztein explicitly rejects a simple definition of jouissance as pleasure or even as suffering. In this passage it is a place, the site at which being persists against the signifier's production of Non-Being. Without that place the universe would be "vain": empty, without consistency, value or foundation.

The subject's being is therefore localized not in a positive essence but in the disturbance that prevents Non-Being from being pure. Eidelsztein connects this with the superego. Each prohibition of drive satisfaction is itself heard as a voice; the subject can localize itself in that very clamoring prohibition as jouissance. He also notes Lacan's play between `jouissance` and "I hear" in French.

[FIGURE: Schema 7, `S(Ⱥ)`, jouissance, voice and superego]
Source location: printed p. 251 / PDF p. 251
Type: closed/interior-eight rendering of graph pathways
Description: an outer loop passes through `S(Ⱥ)` and is labeled "Jouissance"; an inner loop passes through `A`, is labeled "Voice", and returns along a lower segment marked "Superego". The two loops are drawn in continuity rather than as independent circuits.
Directional structure: the pathway from the Other through voice/superego is connected topologically to the upper lack-in-the-Other and jouissance route.
Role in Eidelsztein's argument: localizes the subject's being in jouissance and ties that localization to voice, prohibition and the continuity between `A` and `S(Ⱥ)` when the graph is closed as an interior eight.
Fidelity note: visually checked against PDF p. 251; the source itself labels `S(Ⱥ)`, `A`, "Voice", "Superego" and "Jouissance".

### Desire as lack-of-being, jouissance as resistant being

The final contrast gathers the chapter's argument. Earlier Eidelsztein defined the subject as desire through the remainder of need that does not pass into demand. On that side, the subject is lack-of-being: the effect of subtraction and absence introduced by the signifier.

Jouissance gives another localization. Here the body is involved not as lack but as what remains as satisfaction after the signifier's nothingifying operation. Desire and jouissance are therefore not simple opposites of wanting and pleasure. They are two structural localizations of the subject: desire on the side of lack-of-being, jouissance on the side of the being that resists complete reduction to the signifier.

`S(Ⱥ)` holds these questions together. It is the exceptional signifier of lack in the Other, the mark that no final guarantee exists, and the point from which being and jouissance can be reconsidered without restoring a paternal or doctrinal ultimate truth.

## Chapter 14 - `S(Ⱥ)`: Being (res), jouissance and desire (II)

<!--

### From res cogitans to res extensa

Eidelsztein revisits the previous chapter under a modified title: being `(res)`, desire and jouissance. The Cartesian distinction between `res cogitans` and `res extensa` is introduced because the problem of the subject's being cannot be resolved through thought alone. The route must pass from the failure of the cogito to a localization of being in a place, involving body, voice and jouissance.

He begins again with Lacan's proposition that every signifying chain tends to loop its signification. A message is produced when a chain closes. At the lower level of the graph this closure occurs at `s(A)`, signified of the Other. At the upper level, the unconscious chain closes at `S(Ⱥ)`. The disparity is important: the unconscious cannot close on a positive signification because, in the Freudian account Eidelsztein invokes, the unconscious contains representations rather than affects or values. Its message closes at a signifier.

The analytic operation appropriate to this level is reading rather than merely listening. Eidelsztein relates this to Lacan's "agency of the letter": the upper closure is read as the signifier of a lack in the Other, and the lack is specifically inherent in the Other's function as treasure of signifiers.

### The missing signifier corresponds to the questioning subject

When the Other is asked to account for the value of its treasure in relation to a particular subject, one term is necessarily missing: the signifier that would finally account for that subject itself. The subject must in a sense be subtracted from the count. This lack appears on the upper chain and is tied to the drive, which is why the problem necessarily has bodily consequences.

Eidelsztein distinguishes this structural commonality from the particular contents of dreams, slips and jokes. Each analysis has unique signifiers, but every unconscious message shares the property that no total battery can supply the signifier that would exhaustively represent the subject. He compares this level of formal commonality with Freud's extraction of sexuality and death from the Signorelli forgetting.

`S(Ⱥ)` therefore does not mean that the Other simply does not exist. The Other operates and is a condition of subjectivity. What does not exist is an Other of the Other, a guarantee that would make `A` identical to itself. Eidelsztein extends the same structure to the signifier and to truth: there is no `S = S` that closes difference, and there is no truth that can certify itself as the truth of truth.

Psychoanalysis differs from religion or magic not by announcing as a final doctrine that no ultimate truth exists, but by refusing to turn that absence of guarantee into its own ultimate guarantee. Its question is how the inconsistency of the Other determines the subject's position.

### The being-question and the voice

Because thought is signifier-dependent and signifier-dependent thought necessarily encounters the lack in the Other, the subject cannot exhaust being through the cogito. The analytic question becomes "What am I?" rather than a Cartesian proof of existence.

Eidelsztein rereads Lacan's definition of the signifier in two ways: the signifier represents the subject for another signifier, and the exceptional signifier makes possible the representation of the subject by all the others. The latter function is general to subjectivity, not the case-specific content of a particular individual's unconscious.

Lacan's statement that "I am in the place from which a voice is heard" moves the argument from thinking to place. The signifier creates Non-Being by killing or nullifying the thing, but that nullification is impure. The cry can be transformed into a call, yet something of the cry remains. Eidelsztein identifies this remainder in speech as voice, an object that accompanies signification without itself being a signification.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, voice and the pathway between desire and upper graph]

Role in Eidelsztein's argument: spatially connects the lower desire problem with the voice as what resists the signifier's nullifying action.
Fidelity note: source figure visually inspected; interpretation follows the surrounding text rather than guessing unlabeled geometry.

The place where the signifier's production of Non-Being fails is jouissance. Eidelsztein again insists that jouissance here is not ordinary enjoying. It is a place structurally determined by the symbolic, the point at which something of being resists being reduced to nothing by the signifier. Voice is one exemplary form of this resistant remainder.

<!--

### From "I enjoy this" to jouissance as place

Eidelsztein parallels the correction already made in the theory of desire. Just as Lacanian desire cannot be reduced to the neurotic formula "I desire this", Lacanian jouissance cannot be reduced to "I enjoy with this". The universe would not become meaningless merely because a subject gave up a symptom or a favored satisfaction. What would make it "vain" is the absence of the structural place where the signifier's nullification fails.

The voice comes from the Other, yet the subject must take responsibility for the place of jouissance. This does not make jouissance a possession. Eidelsztein uses Lacan's distinction between incompleteness and inconsistency: the lack of jouissance makes the Other inconsistent in the logical sense that identity cannot simply close on itself.

The subject cannot shift responsibility for this place onto a guaranteed Other because there is no Other of the Other. The structure of "original sin" is therefore introduced as a formal problem of fault. The French `faute` means both lack and fault. What is lacking on the side of the Other falls to the subject not only as desire but also as culpability. Superego and unconscious guilt can thus be derived from the structural lack rather than from a prior moral law imposed from outside.

### Law is grounded in the impossibility of saying jouissance

Eidelsztein reverses the usual causal sequence. It is not paternal Law that first bars access to an otherwise available jouissance. The speaking subject's access to jouissance is already structurally interrupted because saying it submits it to the signifier's nullifying operation. Moral prohibition can take hold because this prior impossibility is already there.

Even if the law commanded "Enjoy!", the subject's response "I hear" would insert the signifier between command and jouissance. The command could neither force jouissance nor abolish its loss. This is the sense in which jouissance is `interdite`: it cannot be fully said and appears only "between the lines". Eidelsztein derives the paternal interdict from this structural inter-dit rather than treating paternal prohibition as the original cause.

### Pleasure as limit of jouissance

Lacan's claim that pleasure limits jouissance produces two different limits. One is the bodily bond with life, obscure and contestable because the real capacities of the body can always be tested again. The other is the signifying regulation Freud calls the pleasure principle, which appears as an explicit law and thus functions as an indisputable prohibition within the symbolic order.

Jouissance is therefore what escapes complete nullification by the signifier, the bodily "bone" or core that remains. Yet it is not limitless. The body supplies a contingent and uncertain limit, while the law of pleasure supplies a formal signifying limit.

### Demand, jouissance and desire as a Möbius structure

Eidelsztein concludes by replacing the earlier trio need-demand-desire with demand-jouissance-desire. The same Möbius logic applies. Desire and jouissance are inverse varieties of what escapes the signifier: desire as lack-of-being, jouissance as what of the body is not nullified.

[FIGURE: Schema 2, demand-jouissance-desire Möbius sequence]

Directional structure: jouissance and desire are linked through the inversion produced by Demand/signifier rather than arranged as independent substances.

Demand belongs to the signifying operation; desire and jouissance designate two structurally opposed effects at its limits. This prepares the final chapter's return to castration, where the lack in the Other and the subject's bodily/phallic position are brought together.

## Chapter 15 - The castration complex in Lacan's teaching

<!--
CHAPTER: 15
PDF_PAGES: 266-271
PRINTED_PAGES: 267-272
STATUS: COMPLETE
-->

### Castration as the Freudian response to the problem of pleasure and jouissance

Eidelsztein devotes the final chapter to the closing pages of Lacan's "Subversion of the Subject" and treats the castration complex as Freud's heteroclite, unexpectedly radical response to the problem opened by the pleasure principle. The law does not first create the barred subject by forbidding an otherwise naturally accessible jouissance. Rather, pleasure already limits jouissance, and castration marks the structural consequences of that limit.

The castration complex is therefore approached as the mark of the interdiction of infinite jouissance. Eidelsztein insists on the double meaning of `interdit`: prohibition and inter-said, what can only be articulated between the lines. The point is not simply that infinite jouissance is morally prohibited. It receives a mark in the signifier. This immediately knots the Freudian castration complex to Lacan's `S(Ⱥ)`, the signifier of a lack in the Other.

### Sacrifice and the choice of the phallus as symbol

Lacan's formulation adds that the mark requires a sacrifice, made in the same act in which its symbol is chosen. That symbol is the phallus. Eidelsztein relates the operation to the `Aufhebung` described in "The Signification of the Phallus": the phallus is raised to the status of symbol, and that symbolic gain entails a loss.

The choice is not simply an individual biographical preference. The phallus is a historically recurrent cultural symbol, and Eidelsztein asks what in the structure makes it apt for this role. Lacan's answer is that the phallus, understood here as the image of the penis, is negativity in its place within the specular image. The relevant "organ" is precisely what cannot be positively secured as the value of the subject's own mirror image.

The child cannot see in the mirror the value its image has for the maternal Other. To apprehend that value it must turn away from the mirror image and seek in the Other the desire that confers significance on the image. The phallus is therefore associated with a blind spot in specular capture, with what is absent at the very place where it would be expected.

Eidelsztein carefully distinguishes this non-specularity from object `a`. The phallus is a hole or blind spot in the specular image. Object `a` can have an image, but the image is structurally different from object `a` as cause. The topological notion of specularity is needed: a left-twisted Möbius strip reflected in a mirror becomes a right-twisted strip that cannot be continuously transformed into the original. Non-specularity is thus a structural mismatch, not merely invisibility.

This also corrects a post-Freudian reading of "His Majesty the Baby". The phrase does not primarily name an infant's own omnipotent narcissism. The parents confer the majestic position. The clinically decisive narcissism is therefore tied to the Other's investment, not simply to an autonomous self-love that analysis should attack.

### Desire as defence and the two ways of concealing castration

The phallus is predestined to embody jouissance in the dialectic of desire because it occupies this negative place. When jouissance is articulated to desire, it is embodied through the sacrificed part. Desire can therefore function as a defence and prohibition against going beyond a certain limit in jouissance.

Eidelsztein makes the relation reciprocal. Desire can defend against jouissance, but jouissance can also defend against desire. The two defences conceal castration differently. Jouissance can use its object to obscure object `a` as cause of desire; desire can use lack to conceal the interdiction of infinite jouissance.

He then compares the older need-demand-desire triad with the newer jouissance-demand-desire triad.

[FIGURE: Schema 1, need/demand/desire and jouissance/demand/desire]

In "The Signification of the Phallus", sexual relation occupies the field of desire because neither biological need nor demand for love is sufficient. Each partner must come to function as cause of the other's desire. The passage is bidirectional: demand transforms need and produces desire, while desire returns through demand to the body as a demand that the body be capable of entering the sexual relation.

Eidelsztein treats the move from need-demand-desire to jouissance-demand-desire as a major theoretical change. The body is no longer the mythical biological body of need. It is the body insofar as the desire of the Other inscribes a lack in the subject's own body, formalized by the phallic absence in the specular field.

### Symbolic sacrifice, imaginary instrument and the knot of registers

Lacan requires a distinction between the symbolic principle of sacrifice and the imaginary function that supplies its instrument while simultaneously veiling its symbolic basis. The phallic image is governed by a symbolic law, yet the same image can conceal that law by making the problem seem to concern anatomy or visual presence alone.

Eidelsztein therefore refuses a hierarchy in which the Symbolic simply dominates the Imaginary. The registers determine and veil one another. The phallus is a knot: the imaginary image of the penis supplies an instrument for a symbolic operation whose consequences extend into the Real of jouissance.

The imaginary function at stake is Freud's narcissistic investment of the object. Lacan reworks it through the specular image `i(a)` as the channel by which bodily libido is transferred to objects. But something is preserved from this mirror immersion. Eidelsztein uses the topological sense of immersion: moving an object into another spatial legality can change its structure. A mirror transformation is not neutral when the object is non-orientable or topologically asymmetric.

The preserved part is where autoeroticism concentrates. This initially seems paradoxical because the missing part of the mirror image was just linked to the desire of the Other. Eidelsztein's resolution is that human autoeroticism is profoundly marked by alterity. In masturbation, the subject seeks in the body precisely what escapes complete imaginary capture, and that bodily act is itself inscribed by the Other. The Rat Man displaying his erection to the ghost of his father is used as an example of this "alloerotic" marking of autoeroticism.

### `-φ`, the missing phallic image and the fantasy of caducity

The anatomical position of the penis at the body's "tip" predisposes it to what Lacan calls a fantasy of caducity or decrepitude: falling off, expiring, becoming impotent. Eidelsztein connects this to its exclusion from the specular image. The phallus, in relation to the penis, is the lost part of the body at the imaginary level.

The vocabulary of caducity also links the phallus to Lacan's lamella discussion. Yet Eidelsztein preserves a distinction: the lamella concerns a lost part of one's own body, while the decidua or expired membranes concern a part lost from the Other's body. Similar images of loss must not be collapsed into one object-theory.

Lacan's formula makes the erectile organ symbolize the place of jouissance not as a positive organ or image but as the part lacking in the desired image. Eidelsztein extracts three coordinated dimensions of the phallus:

- Imaginary: `-φ`, the missing part of the desired/specular image.
- Symbolic: `-1`, the inherence of the missing signifier and the mark of lack in the Other.
- Real: the interdiction or structural impossibility of infinite jouissance.

The phallus is therefore a knot among Imaginary, Symbolic and Real, not a synonym for the penis.

### Masturbation, finitude and structural guilt

The phallus knots the prohibition of jouissance, but not simply because of its anatomical form. Autoerotic access to jouissance is finite. It stops. Eidelsztein reads Lacan's joke about the human hand and monkey hand in this context: anatomy supplies a pathway, but it does not yield infinite jouissance.

The stronger phallic knot occurs through guilt. Masturbatory jouissance frequently carries a structural culpability, especially visible in obsessional complaint even when the subject insists that no empirical other has been harmed. The accusing instance is not "nobody" but the voice of conscience, a superego effect already connected in the previous chapters with voice, prohibition and jouissance.

Lacan's account of guilt therefore knots the real organ, the signifier and its imaginary use. The phallus involves a bodily organ but only through an imaginary-signifying function marked by `-1` and `-φ`.

### From `-φ` to `Φ`: the symbolic phallus as positive mark

The closing move is a change of register. When the phallic image `-φ` passes from the imaginary side of the equation to the symbolic side, it becomes positive `Φ`, the symbolic phallus. It is no longer the absence itself. It is the positive mark of that absence, the signifier of jouissance.

This distinction prevents the conclusion that the phallus simply equals lack. `-1` marks the missing signifier; `-φ` marks the missing phallic image; `Φ` is the symbolic mark produced from that lack. As signifier of jouissance, `Φ` marks both that jouissance is not infinite and that the signifying order itself is not all. Jouissance has left a positive mark that limits the fantasy of a total signifier.

The final movement therefore returns the whole course to `S(Ⱥ)`. The direction of the analysis is not exhausted by discovering what the Other lacks. It reaches the positive formal mark of that lack and the way the subject's desire, fantasy, drive, body and jouissance are organized around it.

Eidelsztein's completed reading of the graph is consequently not a diagrammatic taxonomy. It is a sequence of transformations: from signification and demand to desire and fantasy, from fantasy to drive, from drive to the lack in the Other, and from that lack to the phallic marking of jouissance and castration.

## Internal cross-reference index

This index is retrieval-oriented. Chapter references identify where a concept is developed substantially rather than every passing occurrence.

- **Graph of desire, overall architecture:** Chapters 1, 4, 6-15. Chapter 1 establishes its topological and graph-theoretical status; Chapters 4, 6 and 7 reconstruct Graphs 1-3; Chapters 8-15 work with the completed graph.
- **Graph 1 / elementary cell:** Chapter 4. See also Chapter 5 for its limit as a dual demand circuit.
- **Graph 2:** Chapter 6. Main functions: `I(A)`, ideal identification, ego/other relations, symbolic and imaginary circuits.
- **Graph 3:** Chapter 7. Main problem: the question of the Other and the opening onto fantasy.
- **Completed graph / Graph 4:** Chapters 8-15. It becomes the framework for symptom, fantasy, drive, `S(Ⱥ)`, jouissance and castration.
- **Topology:** Chapters 1-2, with later applications in Chapters 9-15. Key figures include graph invariants, torus, cuts, interior eight, border and circuit.
- **Mathematical graph theory / nets:** Chapters 1-2. Euler and Koenigsberg, vertices, edges, paths, degree, traversability, connectivity and planarity are used to distinguish topology from representational resemblance.
- **Object `a`:** Chapters 1-2, 7, 9-13. Eidelsztein treats object `a` as structurally inseparable from hole, border, remainder and cause rather than as an ordinary desired object.
- **Other, `A`:** Chapters 3-15. Especially Chapters 3, 5-7 and 13-14 for code, battery/treasure, incompleteness, truth and lack in the Other.
- **`S(Ⱥ)`, signifier of a lack in the Other:** Chapters 1, 6, 8-9 and especially Chapters 13-15. Chapter 13 gives the most sustained formal treatment.
- **Signifier / signified:** Chapters 1, 3-6 and 13. Chapter 1 distinguishes signifier from letter; Chapters 3-4 develop code, message, punctuation and retroaction.
- **Letter / reading:** Chapter 1, with consequences for later mathemes and graph notation.
- **Point de capiton / quilting point:** Chapter 4; the Name-of-the-Father as a stabilizing quilting function is revisited in Chapter 5.
- **Need, demand and desire:** Chapter 3 establishes the sequence; Chapters 4-5 show its limits; Chapters 14-15 recast it alongside jouissance.
- **Desire as beyond demand:** Chapters 3-8, especially Chapters 4 and 7-8.
- **Desire as desire of the Other:** Chapter 7, with continuations in Chapters 8-10.
- **`Che vuoi?` / the question:** Chapter 7, continued through fantasy in Chapter 8.
- **Symptom:** Chapter 8, with earlier preparation in Chapters 3-4 and later relation to fantasy and desire.
- **Fantasy / fantasme:** Chapters 7-12. Chapters 8-10 are central; Chapter 10 analyzes the fantasy formula, frame, border and scene.
- **Fantasy formula, barred subject and object `a`:** Chapters 9-12. Chapter 10 gives the most explicit logical treatment of the lozenge.
- **Drive formula and drive circuit:** Chapters 10-12. Chapter 11 rejects an organic-energy model; Chapter 12 develops the circuit, perversion and partial drive.
- **Erogenous zone / border / cut:** Chapters 10-12.
- **Ego, `m`, and image of the other, `i(a)`:** Chapter 6, with the imaginary circuit revisited in Chapters 8-9.
- **Ego Ideal / `I(A)`:** Chapter 6. Eidelsztein reads the formula as the One of the Other and links it to petrification in an ideal.
- **Ideal ego:** Chapter 6, as imaginary response to symbolic alienation.
- **Neurosis and psychosis:** Chapters 4-5; later structural contrasts appear in Chapters 11-12.
- **Hysteria and obsession:** Chapter 5 for different responses to structural lack; Chapters 8-9 for positions toward desire and fantasy.
- **Perversion:** Chapters 10-12, especially the inversion of the fantasy relation and the position of the subject as object-cause.
- **Truth:** Chapters 4 and 6, then Chapters 13-14 in relation to the absence of a final guarantee.
- **Name-of-the-Father:** Chapter 5, reconsidered in Chapter 13 as distinct from `S(Ⱥ)` and from an Other of the Other.
- **No Other of the Other:** Chapter 13, continued in Chapter 14.
- **Being / lack-of-being:** Chapters 13-14.
- **Jouissance:** Chapters 1, 5 and 13-15. Chapters 13-14 localize jouissance in relation to `S(Ⱥ)`, voice, law and the limits of signification.
- **Voice:** Chapters 1 and 13-14, especially as object and as a function connecting the Other to jouissance.
- **Superego:** Chapters 13-14.
- **Law / interdiction / inter-said:** Chapters 4-5 and 14-15.
- **Phallus:** Chapters 8 and 15. Chapter 15 distinguishes `-φ` from `Φ` and rejects the equation of the phallus with an ordinary object.
- **Castration:** Chapter 15, prepared by the upper-left and upper-right relations of the graph throughout the book.
- **Analysis, direction of the cure and end of analysis:** Chapters 7-10 and 13-15. The book repeatedly treats the graph as a pathway rather than as a static classificatory diagram.

## Provenance / source note

All substantive reconstruction in this file is based on Alfredo Eidelsztein's *The Graph of Desire: Using the Work of Jacques Lacan*, Karnac Books English edition, 2009, from the project PDF `the-graph-of-desire-using-the-work-of-jacques-lacan.pdf`.

This is a reconstruction of Eidelsztein's lectures and arguments. References to Lacan and Freud are reported as Eidelsztein deploys them. They were not silently harmonized against other project editions. The file should therefore be used as a technical guide to Eidelsztein's reading of the graph, not as a substitute for primary Lacan when establishing what Lacan himself wrote or said.

## Processing notes and uncertainties

The PDF contains a usable text layer for ordinary prose but corrupts a number of mathematically or typographically significant symbols. Production therefore used native extraction for prose and targeted visual inspection for consequential diagrams and notation. No global OCR was performed.

The notation `S(Ⱥ)` has been normalized in this reconstruction after visual verification of the barred `A` in source figures. The ordinary text extraction frequently rendered the same symbol as `S(~)` or other corrupted variants. The same principle was used for barred subject notation, drive/fantasy formulas and phallic notation when the source was visually recoverable.

Important diagrams are represented by descriptive `[FIGURE: ...]` blocks rather than redrawn graphics. These descriptions record visible labels, directional structure and the role of the figure in Eidelsztein's argument. They should not be treated as facsimile reproductions.

No material unresolved source uncertainty remains that changes the chapter-level reconstruction. Minor typographic details in low-resolution formulas that are not required for the conceptual argument are left descriptive rather than guessed.
